# Workspace and Model Operating Policy

## Storage topology

- **C: is the active development home.** Build, edit, test, serve, and deploy coding projects from local C-drive folders.
- Default project root: `[user home]\Projects`.
- Existing canonical saake.dev source remains `[Claude research]\site` until deliberately relocated.
- **Z: is not a development runtime.** Use it for the Obsidian vault, learning/reference material, archives, and after-the-fact backups.
- Never run Node/Next/Python development servers from Z:.
- Never treat a Z-drive mirror as authoritative unless Aryan explicitly changes this policy.

## Model routing

| Role | Model | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Coordinator / lead | `gpt-5.6-sol` | Heavy reasoning, orchestration, audits, ambiguous work, decisions |
| Implementation worker | `gpt-5.6-terra` | Long, well-specified coding and routine execution |
| Bug investigator | `gpt-5.6-luna` | High-volume debugging, testing, bug discovery, log/code analysis |
| Architecture council | `claude-opus-5 [1M]` | Exceptional whole-project architecture and highest-tier planning |

Rules:

- SOL remains Hermes's global primary.
- Terra remains SOL's only automatic fallback.
- Luna and Opus are explicitly assigned workers, not automatic fallbacks.
- Explicitly pin and verify models for CLI/delegated work.
- Never silently use DeepSeek or unrelated models.

## Backup policy

The former hourly `CloudWorkspace Backup to RaiDrive` scheduled task was disabled on 2026-08-17 because it launched an interactive terminal every hour. A future backup system must run hidden, incrementally, and only after its scope and resource usage are intentionally designed.

## Creator description

Most people use AI coding agents by giving them one giant prompt and letting them run wild. That might work for a tiny project, but it quickly falls apart when you are building real software.

In this video, I walk through my complete AI development workflow using agents, specifications, roadmaps, testing, pull requests, CI, security scanning, and independent code reviews. I also demonstrate the process on a real project, from the initial request through review, fixes, validation, and the final merge.

The model matters, but your workflow matters more. Manual gates, clear acceptance criteria, small pull requests, and proper testing are what turn AI-generated code into maintainable software.

What does your AI development workflow look like? Let me know what you would add or change.

# 4 AI Agents To Automate 99% Of Your Life

[Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TL8V41Ea6oM) · **Sandeep Swadia** · **20:46**

## Creator description

Join my free newsletter: https://sandeepswadia.beehiiv.com/

Take us on your morning run or commute, follow us on Spotify:  https://open.spotify.com/show/033nSSACs3S4g5NUIrXnHx

Everyone's talking about AI agents like they're some far-off, technical thing. They're not. You've probably already used one without knowing it, and by the end of this episode, you'll have built four of your own.

In this episode, I walk through the Four Cs framework, coordination, creativity, clarity, and coaching, and show you exactly how to build an agent for each one.

You'll learn how to:

- Build a coordination agent so your inbox and calendar stop running your day for you
- Build a creativity agent that helps you go from rough notes to a finished deck, while every real decision still stays yours
- Build a clarity agent that turns a confusing contract or policy into a plain-English table of risks and obligations
- Build a coaching agent that rehearses your hardest conversations with you, out loud, before you ever walk into the real room
- Use one simple prompt structure across every agent: the job, the tool, the categories, the output, and the boundary
- Know when to keep an agent on a short leash and when it's earned more responsibility

I also share Ed Catmull's philosophy on early rough cuts at Pixar, Microsoft's data on how often we get interrupted during the workday, a JDP survey on interview anxiety, and why comparisons to Charlie Chaplin's Modern Times still hold up nearly a century later.

Most importantly, you'll learn that the agents themselves are the easy part. The real edge comes from the judgment you bring to what you delegate and what you don't.

Because it's not really about how powerful your tools are. It's about what you choose to hand off, and what you choose to keep.

CREATIVITY (Document Generation)     │     ├── Point LLM to local working directory.     │     ├── Supply raw/messy notes + output constraints (target audience, slide count).     │     └── Trigger file generation skills (e.g., .pptx, .docx) -> Iteratively refine.     │     ├── 3. CLARITY (Information Extraction)     │     ├── Telescope Mode: Cross-search web + Drive + emails for macro-summary.     │     └── Microscope Mode: Extract legal/dense docs into a 5-column risk/summary matrix.     │     └── 4. COACHING (Voice Simulation)           ├── Load context (resume, job description, company details).           ├── Set adversarial persona prompt (e.g., skeptical hiring manager).           ├── Engage via real-time audio voice mode -> Request post-session critique sheet. Key Prompts & Configs 1. 5-Part Email Triage Prompt:  "Review my unread Gmail from the last 24 hours. Sort it into three buckets: urgent, informational, and ignore. For anything urgent, draft a reply that sounds like me. Don't send anything without my approval."  2. Calendar Conflict Prompt:  "Look at my Google Calendar for today and tomorrow. Compare it against all the urgent emails that you found. Organize my day by telling me what creates conflict in my schedule, what needs an action or prep before a meeting, and what can wait."  3. Contract "Microscope" Extraction Prompt:  "Read this document carefully. Find the key terms like fee structure, obligations, deadlines, exclusions, and risks. Pay attention to anything that's unclear or anything that makes me liable. Create a table with five columns: What the contract says | What it means in plain English | Why it matters | Risk level | Questions I should be asking."  4. **[00:00]** Tax season is right around the corner,

**[00:01]** and most people's scrambling to do their

**[00:03]** taxes just end up paying three to $500

**[00:05]** for an accountant they might see once a

**[00:07]** year. Or, they spend three to five hours

**[00:09]** fighting TurboTax and getting hit with

**[00:11]** add-ons at the end. And sadly, the IRS

**[00:13]** makes this feel complicated on purpose.

**[00:15]** So, that companies like TurboTax and H&R

**[00:17]** Block can make money off your confusion.

**[00:18]** So, I thought, what if I could just get

**[00:20]** Claude to do it for me and show you how

**[00:22]** to do it? So, we'll be doing this in

**[00:23]** three steps: the GPS framework and get

**[00:25]** AI to file your taxes. Let me break

**[00:27]** these down. So, first, G is gather.

**[00:30]** Before anyone touches your taxes, you

**[00:31]** need the right documents. So, like your

**[00:33]** W-2, like your job income, anything you

**[00:35]** earn on the side, some mortgage docs, or

**[00:37]** if you made any donations. This is what

**[00:38]** you're normally paying your accountants

**[00:40]** to chase you for. That's the gather

**[00:41]** phase, and I'll show you how you can get

**[00:43]** Claude to help you with all of these,

**[00:44]** gather all your docs, and put it in one

**[00:45]** place. Then, we move on to process, P.

**[00:48]** This is where the accountant takes all

**[00:49]** the information they gathered and then

**[00:51]** compile it into one government document

**[00:53]** called a Form 1040. Don't worry about

**[00:55]** it, but I'll show you how Claude can

**[00:56]** make it do that as well. Now, after it's

**[00:58]** processed, we need to send this to the

**[01:00]** IRS. So, there's a service called

**[01:01]** FreeTaxUSA we can use, but you need to

**[01:03]** fill in all your details, which is

**[01:05]** pretty tedious. So, we can get Claude to

**[01:07]** open up FreeTaxUSA in the browser, log

**[01:09]** in, and fill out every field

**[01:11]** automatically, so you can review it. And

**[01:12]** even if you have zero technical

**[01:14]** background, you'll be able to do this,

**[01:15]** because all we're going to be doing is

**[01:17]** simply speaking to Claude. Now, to walk

**[01:19]** through this properly, we're going to do

**[01:20]** this for a real person. Well, a fake

**[01:22]** person. I can't do my own taxes on

**[01:24]** camera, so we're going to be using Alex.

**[01:25]** So, let's say Alex is a 35-year-old

**[01:27]** marketing coordinator. He makes $65,000

**[01:29]** a year. And to add some complexity for

**[01:32]** Claude, let's say he owns a home, so he

**[01:34]** has a mortgage and mortgage interest he

# How to Build $10,000 Agentic Workflows (Claude Code Tutorial) — raw transcript



> [!note] Raw evidence

> Timestamped captions exported without summarization from the preserved local mcptube database snapshot.



**[00:00]** Agentic workflows are not just a trend.

**[00:01]** They're the future of the AI industry.

**[00:03]** More and more companies are making the

**[00:04]** shift to agentic workflows, and this is

**[00:06]** just getting started because it's

**[00:07]** estimated that the AI agentic market is

**[00:09]** going from about $7 billion this year to

**[00:11]** around 93 billion in the next couple of

**[00:13]** years. So, I can tell you right now that

**[00:14]** knowing how to build agentic workflows

**[00:16]** is going to be one of the most valuable

**[00:18]** skills that you can have. So, in this

**[00:19]** video, I'm going to break down why you

**[00:20]** should be building agentic workflows,

**[00:22]** and then I'm going to actually build one

**[00:23]** live in front of you so you can see

**[00:25]** exactly how it works. And by the end,

**[00:26]** I'll show you how to actually sell these

**[00:28]** if you want to make some money with your

**[00:29]** skills. So, let's get into it. So,

**[00:30]** before we build anything, I want to show

**[00:32]** you why this all matters because it's

**[00:33]** not just hype. This is real money moving

**[00:35]** into real technology. Right now, the

**[00:37]** agentic AI market is sitting at around

**[00:39]** $8 billion. By 2030, that's expected to

**[00:41]** hit 40 to 50 billion. That's not just a

**[00:43]** small jump. That's an entire industry

**[00:44]** being built in front of our eyes. And

**[00:46]** it's not just projections. About 25% of

**[00:48]** enterprises are already deploying

**[00:49]** agentic pilots this year, and by 2027,

**[00:51]** that number will jump to 50%. So, half

**[00:54]** of major companies will be running some

**[00:55]** version of agentic workflows within the

**[00:57]** next 2 years. And with that comes

**[00:58]** massive budget allocations, new security

**[01:00]** requirements, and a ton of new

**[01:01]** opportunities for people who know how to

**[01:03]** build these systems. So, why is this

**[01:04]** happening now? What's driving the shift?

**[01:06]** It comes down to pretty much one thing,

**[01:07]** which is companies are starting to hit

**[01:08]** that ceiling of what traditional

**[01:10]** automation can do, and they're starting

**[01:11]** to realize they could move a lot faster

**[01:13]** with more agentic workflows. If you've

**[01:15]** been building workflows in tools like

**[01:16]** end-to-end or Zapier, you know the

**[01:18]** drill. You map out every step, you

**[01:19]** connect the different nodes or blocks,

**[01:20]** you handle the edge cases yourself, and

**[01:22]** it works until it breaks because

**[01:23]** traditional workflows will break when

**[01:25]** they hit something unexpected. And when

**[01:26]** that happens, someone has to usually go

**[01:28]** in manually and fix that. And that's

**[01:30]** maintenance. That's time. That's

**[01:31]** ultimately money. Now, I do want to be

**[01:32]** real with you here because there's a lot

**[01:33]** of noise online about agentic workflows

**[01:35]** that makes it sound like they're just

**[01:36]** completely magic and they fix themselves

**[01:38]** forever, and that is partially true, but

**[01:39]** only in a specific context, at least

**[01:41]** right now. Cuz when you're actively

**[01:43]** working in a tool at Cloud Code and you

**[01:44]** trigger a workflow yourself and say,

**[01:46]** "Hey, go research these competitors and

**[01:48]** build me a report," the agent is sitting

**[01:49]** right there with you. So, if something

**[01:50]** breaks, the agent can catch it mid-run,

**[01:52]** it can adjust its approach, it can

**[01:53]** update its tools, and keep going. That

**[01:55]** self-healing piece is very, very real,

**[01:57]** and it's incredibly powerful while

**[01:58]** you're building and while you're

**[01:59]** iterating. But, once you deploy that

**[02:01]** workflow to run on its own, on a

**[02:02]** schedule or triggered by a webhook or

**[02:04]** something like that, that is when you're

**[02:06]** deploying the code, you're deploying the

**[02:07]** tools, not the actual agent itself. So,

**[02:10]** if you've seen my previous videos where

**[02:11]** we've used the WAT framework, we are

**[02:13]** basically deploying the W workflows and

**[02:15]** the T tools, but not the A agent. But,

**[02:18]** I'll cover this more in depth later

**[02:19]** during the live build if you're

**[02:20]** confused. What this means is that the

**[02:21]** self-healing ability ultimately goes

**[02:23]** away when the code is up in the cloud,

**[02:26]** you know, running automatically. And at

**[02:27]** that point it does behave more like a

**[02:28]** traditional automation, but that's

**[02:29]** really a good thing because automations

**[02:31]** are predictable, they're deterministic,

**[02:33]** and those types are the best ones. So,

**[02:34]** then where's the real advantage? Really,

**[02:36]** it sits in how you build. Traditional

**[02:38]** automation is like building a train

**[02:39]** track by hand. You're laying every rail,

**[02:41]** every switch, every connection all by

**[02:43]** yourself. Whereas, with Agentic

**[02:44]** workflows, it's like you're just telling

**[02:45]** a construction crew, "Hey, I need you to

**[02:47]** build a train track from here to there."

**[02:48]** And then they build it for you. Meaning,

**[02:50]** if they hit a problem during

**[02:51]** construction, they would figure it out.

**[02:52]** So, you end up with a better train

**[02:54]** track, it's built faster with fewer

**[02:55]** mistakes because the agent handled the

**[02:57]** edge cases during the build process that

**[02:59]** you might have missed or not thought of.

**[03:00]** And then the idea is you battle test it

**[03:02]** before you ever actually deploy it. So,

**[03:04]** then you have a lot of confidence that

**[03:05]** it will always work. So, in our train

**[03:06]** analogy, before we deploy that train

**[03:08]** track, we would have like 10 different

**[03:10]** types of trains test drive on it. They

**[03:12]** would be different weights, different

**[03:13]** lengths, and maybe different wheels. And

**[03:14]** we want to make sure that our track can

**[03:16]** work for all different types of trains

**[03:17]** before we deploy it. And the reason this

**[03:18]** is actually possible now is because the

**[03:20]** technology is finally caught up. LLMs

**[03:22]** have gotten really reliable enough to

**[03:23]** use in production and we're not just

**[03:25]** playing around with chatbots anymore.

**[03:26]** These models can reason, they can make

**[03:27]** decisions, and they can execute

**[03:29]** multi-step tasks with real consistency.

**[03:31]** On top of that, we've got things to use

**[03:32]** like skills or MCP or A2A. We've also

**[03:35]** got infrastructure like trigger.dev,

**[03:37]** modal, or Vercel that make deployment

**[03:38]** way simpler than it used to be. And most

# Watch Order

A learning path for the 20-video Capture corpus, ordered by prerequisites and practical value rather than capture chronology. This is a guide, not a forced syllabus; skip markers show where a video is redundant if you already know a concept.

## How to use this

- Videos marked **watch** are core.
- Videos marked **optional** can be skipped or scanned.
- Long courses have chapter targets, not full-length demands.
- After each phase, pause and map what you learned back to your own goals: build a website, automate a workflow, or sell a service.
- Raw transcripts and chapters live in [[AI Learning Library]]; use them to search before watching.

## Phase 0 — Orientation (optional, 1 video)

- `--8pJvYNcX4` — **Every AI Model Explained** · watch if you don't know the difference between flagship/mid-tier/light/specialized models. If you already use models daily, skip.

## Phase 1 — Core mental model (3 videos)

1. `8yE6G1Lup1s` — **Hermes Agent Full Course** · chapters 0–8 are the core: what an agentic harness is, model vs harness, setup, channels, memory, profiles/squads, MCP/CLI/API, cron. This is the single most important frame for your whole library.
2. `TK6R_8ZWSvs` — **Duke Pan AI Workflow** · model/harness/workspace, memory files, knowledge graphs, manager-worker. It directly extends Hermes course concepts with how a senior engineer organizes the workspace.
3. `Aie0nYktsNA` — **ThePrimeagen's New AI Workflow** · short, opinionated counterpoint. Use it to calibrate skepticism: not every workflow step is necessary.

## Phase 2 — Building with an agent (3 videos)

4. `L4g6GGLzAyo` — **Traversy Media: Better Way to Build Software with AI** · the cleanest end-to-end: plans, setup, UI prototype, feature build, tests, deploy. Watch the whole thing.
5. `gpOfsGW1xRk` — **Tech With Tim: My Real AI Coding Workflow** · Cursor setup, context, skills, MCP, rules. Overlaps Traversy on planning/build; adds IDE-specific tooling.
6. `wcRR5P0S2Us` — **Chris Titus: AI Coding Workflow That Actually Works** · guardrails, specs, testing/linting, acceptance criteria, review before merge, CI. The most practical quality layer.

## Phase 3 — Agentic workflows and systems (3 videos)

7. `nQwJVHCtDDY` — **Matt Pocock's Agentic Engineering Workflow** · how a working engineer uses agents in production; watch after you can build a small thing yourself.
8. `vFepZE_wrfg` — **Build $10,000 Agentic Workflows (Claude Code)** · Claude Code setup, controlling the agent, selling the result. Good bridge from building to business.
9. `TL8V41Ea6oM` — **4 AI Agents to Automate 99% of Life** · broader life-automation view; optional if you only care about coding.

## Phase 4 — Memory and persistent systems (2 videos)

10. `R1TNGOZAOZs` — **Hermes Mnemosyne & Hindsight memory tutorial** · foundation-library video that explains the memory layer the newer Hermes course references.
11. `znj-WpMj1dI` — **Obsidian + Agentic AI / LLM Wiki** · the direct predecessor of how this vault works. Watch before you rely on the vault as a knowledge layer.

## Phase 5 — Specialized builds (3 videos)

12. `kKG5MDF_234` — **Tina Huang: Favourite AI Workflow Nobody Talks About** · hyperspecific apps: identify a workflow, map it, build one small app. Excellent template for turning ideas into projects.
13. `p1J5uWcn3hI` — **Kimi K3 Web Design** · design/build a site with an AI model, giving it taste, publishing, SEO. Relevant to saake.dev.
14. `uED-1uD563Y` — **8 Practical Hermes Agent Use Cases** · chapter targets: use cases 1–6. Concrete outputs after you know the core.

## Phase 6 — Content and business (4 videos)

15. `pSnTKR2Phyo` — **Claude Content Creation tutorial** · optional unless you want content workflows.
16. `_gV6pjy8RDU` — **Claude + Higgsfield content creation** · optional; builds on pSnTKR2Phyo.
17. `B6tEsURlM3I` — **Higgsfield Supercomputer** · optional; only if you want AI video workflows.
18. `dfdrJQtFs_w` — **Claude Taxes tutorial** · optional; useful practical workflow, not core to engineering.
19. `KTEe5705RHw` — **Interactive Claude Full Course** · long course; watch Level 4 (Claude Code), Level 5 (agentic workflows), Level 7 (deploy), Level 8 (second brain → side hustle), Level 9 (AI OS) selectively. The rest is demo-heavy and can be skipped.
20. `1N105PDLP2o` — **Clicky computer tutor** · optional; shows a practical agentic tutor use case.

## Redundancy guidance

- `8yE6G1Lup1s` + `TK6R_8ZWSvs` + `Aie0nYktsNA` overlap on "model vs harness." Watch 8yE6G1Lup1s, then use the others as perspective.
- `L4g6GGLzAyo`, `gpOfsGW1xRk`, and `wcRR5P0S2Us` overlap on planning/context/build; the unique value is Traversy (end-to-end), Tech With Tim (IDE/tools), Chris Titus (quality gates).
- `pSnTKR2Phyo` and `_gV6pjy8RDU`/`B6tEsURlM3I` are three content-creation tutorials from the same creator; one is enough unless you want the specific tool.

## Foundation library placement

The 9 older Hermes/Obsidian videos are optional prerequisites. The most useful before the Capture path:

- `R1TNGOZAOZs` (memory) before Phase 4.
- `znj-WpMj1dI` (Obsidian wiki) before Phase 4.
- `QbjAQFJJyt0` (LLM wiki) optional deep dive.
- `GL67DEf2nyI` (Hermes Desktop) optional if you need the desktop UI specifically.
- `4KXLW9Y1r4c` (Ollama local) optional if you want local models.
- `dblWxS_4NZw` (Git & GitHub with AI) optional if you are new to Git.
- `v_E42FkgH2I` (Docker restriction) optional if you care about isolation.
- `OMQo6YMZYzo` (Tailscale) optional if you want remote devices.
- `ZL-8IhjQDvE` (Hermes Supercomputer/Abacus) optional deep dive.

## Next after watching

- Build a small hyper-specific app (Phase 5) with your chosen harness.
- Turn a repeated workflow into a cron job or skill.
- Add memory/knowledge structure to your vault.
- Decide whether the content/business videos support an actual income experiment.

- **Contradiction/tension:** Creators disagree on whether harness/tooling or model matters more; Chris Titus says "models won't save you," while the model-overview video treats model tiers as central.
- **Skip if:** you already understand that the harness orchestrates the model and the model is swappable.

## Planning and specs

- **Strongest source:** `L4g6GGLzAyo` (Traversy) — plans before build, then feature workflow.
- **Reinforcing:** `wcRR5P0S2Us` (specs + acceptance criteria) · `gpOfsGW1xRk` (context/rules).
- **Unique additions:** Chris Titus's acceptance criteria and roadmap gate; Tech With Tim's "provide context" step.
- **Contradiction/tension:** Amount of planning varies: Traversy writes detailed plans; Primeagen appears lighter-weight; Duke Pan favors workspace/memory structures over long prose plans.
- **Skip if:** you already write specs and test before handing work to an agent.

## Context, rules, and agent memory

- **Strongest source:** `gpOfsGW1xRk` (context, skills, MCP, rules) + `TK6R_8ZWSvs` (memory files, knowledge graphs, transcripts).
- **Reinforcing:** `R1TNGOZAOZs` (Hermes memory) · `znj-WpMj1dI` (Obsidian wiki) · `QbjAQFJJyt0` (LLM wiki).
- **Unique additions:** memory is not just chat; it's user identity, durable files, knowledge graphs, and transcript-derived context.
- **Contradiction/tension:** some creators treat context as one prompt; others build persistent knowledge layers. The vault/agent community pushes toward persistent memory, while many coding demos stay prompt-scoped.
- **Skip if:** you already maintain a memory/skill/knowledge structure.

## Skills, MCP, and connectors

- **Strongest source:** `8yE6G1Lup1s` (MCP/CLI/API, skills) + `gpOfsGW1xRk` (agent skills/MCP).
- **Reinforcing:** `KTEe5705RHw` Level 5 (skills + Blotato carousel) · `wcRR5P0S2Us` (agents and skills).
- **Unique additions:** connectors are a spectrum from MCP to CLI to API; skills package reusable procedures.
- **Contradiction/tension:** minimalists avoid heavy connector stacks; automation-focused videos embrace many integrations.
- **Skip if:** you already know how to install/use skills and MCP connectors.

## Testing, review, security

- **Strongest source:** `wcRR5P0S2Us` — lint/test, independent AI review, local review, CI, final merge gate.
- **Reinforcing:** `L4g6GGLzAyo` (unit tests) · `KTEe5705RHw` (Level 9 AI OS / PRD-driven engineering).
- **Unique additions:** Chris Titus's "slow is smooth" and independent reviewer pattern; saake.dev's own AGENTS.md uses the same idea.
- **Contradiction/tension:** speed-focused demos often skip review; quality-focused workflows make review mandatory.
- **Skip if:** you already gate agent changes behind tests/review.

## Manager-worker patterns

- **Strongest source:** `TK6R_8ZWSvs` (manager-worker for automations).
- **Reinforcing:** `8yE6G1Lup1s` (profiles/squads as AI employees) · `TL8V41Ea6oM` (life automation agents).
- **Unique additions:** manager-worker is a repeatable architecture for background automations; squads/profiles formalize it in Hermes.
- **Contradiction/tension:** solo-agent minimalists would argue one good agent with good context beats a manager-worker team; enterprise-leaning creators promote team topology.
- **Skip if:** you already understand orchestration and just need one agent.

## Automation economics and pricing

- **Strongest source:** `vFepZE_wrfg` (why automations break, selling agentic workflows).
- **Reinforcing:** `KTEe5705RHw` Level 8 (website/product/payments/marketing) + selling/pricing section · `axLMgM5NEQg` (7 AI business models, description only).
- **Unique additions:** basic reliability still matters; clients pay for outcomes; offer menus/retainers/risk reversal are recurring pricing patterns.
- **Contradiction/tension:** "automation breaks" warns against overpromising; business videos emphasize speed and opportunity.
- **Skip if:** you are only learning engineering, not building a service business.

## Hyperspecific apps

- **Strongest source:** `kKG5MDF_234` (identify workflow → map it → build small app).
- **Reinforcing:** `p1J5uWcn3hI` (Kimi site build) · `KTEe5705RHw` Level 2 connectors.
- **Unique additions:** one workflow, one small app; don't build a platform first.
- **Contradiction/tension:** hyperspecific app advice contradicts "build a complete product" advice; choose based on whether you are validating or shipping.
- **Skip if:** you already know to start narrow.

## Design taste and website building

- **Strongest source:** `p1J5uWcn3hI` (giving Kimi taste, grading against Big 8, publishing/SEO).
- **Reinforcing:** `KTEe5705RHw` Level 8 (second brain → website/product).
- **Unique additions:** taste is explicitly taught as a design reference, not just code; relevant to saake.dev.
- **Contradiction/tension:** AI-generated site speed vs hand-crafted design quality is a recurring tension across the corpus.
- **Skip if:** you are not building web assets.

## Content creation workflows

- **Strongest source:** `pSnTKR2Phyo` (Claude content creation) · `_gV6pjy8RDU` (Claude + Higgsfield).
- **Reinforcing:** `B6tEsURlM3I` (Higgsfield supercomputer) · `KTEe5705RHw` Level 4 (carousels).
- **Unique additions:** two-pass editing (cut + B-roll), content repurposing octopus, auto-posting calendars.
- **Contradiction/tension:** the "Just Changed Forever" titles overstate novelty; treat as tutorials, not news.
- **Skip if:** content creation is not your goal.

## Memory/knowledge layer in Obsidian

- **Strongest source:** `znj-WpMj1dI` (Obsidian + agentic AI wiki prep) · `QbjAQFJJyt0` (LLM wiki).
- **Reinforcing:** `R1TNGOZAOZs` (memory) · `TK6R_8ZWSvs` (knowledge graphs/transcripts) · `8yE6G1Lup1s` (user.md, soul.md, Honcho).

# AI Learning Library

A durable research corpus built from the YouTube links Aryan dropped into the Telegram Capture channel, plus an older Hermes/Obsidian foundation set. The purpose is **preservation and navigation first**: extract raw evidence now; process and synthesize later.

## Start here

1. [[Watch Order]] — prerequisite-aware viewing path
2. [[Overlap Map]] — repeated ideas, contradictions, and what each source uniquely adds
3. [[Capture Ledger]] — every captured URL and exact extraction status
4. [[Processing Queue]] — unresolved transcripts and future analysis work

## Corpus boundaries

- **Capture curriculum:** 20 YouTube links captured by Aryan on 2026-08-16.
- **Foundation library:** 9 earlier Hermes/Obsidian/Git/memory videos captured on 2026-08-13.
- **Excluded:** unrelated local media files, private videos, and anything not sourced from the Capture channel or the prior learning-library ingest.

## Evidence layers

- `Sources/` — one navigable evidence record per captured video: metadata, description, chapters, bounded public-comment sample, extraction status, and raw pointers.
- `Raw Transcripts/` — exact timestamped transcripts exported from a preserved local mcptube database snapshot. No summarization.
- `Raw Metadata/` — machine-readable JSON from the local library.
- `Raw Export Manifest.json` — deterministic inventory of exported records.
- `Source Note Manifest.json` — one-to-one source-note manifest.

## Rules for this library

- Raw corpus first, enrichment later.
- A zero-segment transcript is **not** complete.
- Never delete/re-add a known-good video to trigger processing.
- Descriptions, transcripts, creator chapters, and comments are distinct evidence types.
- Comments are a bounded public sample, not a representative survey.
- Every interpretive claim should point back to a video ID and timestamp where the transcript allows it.
- Prefer simple local tools (`sqlite`, `yt-dlp`, Markdown, JSON) over API-heavy systems.

## Current verified coverage

- 20 Capture-channel links expected.
- 17 are present in the preserved local library snapshot.
- 16 Capture videos have non-empty transcripts from that snapshot.
- 3 additional Capture transcripts were recovered non-destructively from English automatic captions.

notes.body:
# saake.dev Brain Control Plane

The canonical saake.dev site now includes a local, manually refreshed control plane at `/brain`.

## Architecture

- **Vault index** — generated from `[Obsidian vault]`.
- **Action surface** — active threads, folder areas, tags, backlinks, and searchable note cards.
- **Research archive** — Markdown handovers, plans, audits, and walkthroughs from `[Claude research]` plus selected Antigravity brain artifacts.
- **Agent control plane** — the page records the intended manager/subagent split: `gpt-5.6-sol` as manager and `gpt-5.6-terra` for bounded subagent work.

## Manual refresh

Run from the canonical site on the local NTFS drive:

```text
npm run brain:sync
```

The combined refresh and verification command is:

```text
npm run brain:check
```

The manual upgrade pass is:

```text
npm run brain:upgrade
```

That command runs three parallel read-only `gpt-5.6-terra` audits (vault curation, design, and reliability), then asks a pinned `gpt-5.6-sol` manager to synthesize the next implementation slice. Reports are saved under `.brain\upgrades\`; the manager is forbidden from editing during this audit pass.

The generated snapshot is `content\brain-data.json`. It is derived data and must not be edited by hand.

## Safety boundaries

- The Brain is **private/local by default**. Normal production builds omit Brain navigation, sitemap entries, and generated Brain pages unless `ENABLE_PRIVATE_BRAIN=1` is explicitly set.
- `Private/` and `ReadOnly/` vault content is excluded by the generator in every mode.
- `npm run brain:sync` creates the private local snapshot. `npm run brain:sync:public` is fail-closed: only notes with `publish: true` are eligible, and the raw Claude research archive is excluded.
- Generated snapshots and `.brain/upgrades/` reports are Git-ignored.
- Generated JSON and rendered pages contain source-relative references only; absolute Windows paths are not emitted.
- Sync fails if a required source is unavailable and writes atomically, preserving the previous valid snapshot on failure.
- The public portfolio verification scans do not treat archived Brain documents as live portfolio claims; every Brain page carries a `data-brain-archive` marker.
- The canonical site remains on `C:`. RaiDrive `Z:` is a source/archive surface, not the active build workspace.

## Verified snapshot

On 2026-08-16, the private sync indexed 83 vault notes and 99 Claude/Antigravity research artifacts across 12 folders and 40 tags. `npm run brain:check` generated 200 static pages and passed build, no-JS, fabrication, accessibility, canonical, archive-label, share-card, contrast, and bundle-weight checks. The normal public production gate also passed while omitting private Brain content. The independent contrast gate passed with a minimum measured ratio of 5.34:1.

A real `npm run brain:upgrade` pass completed with all three `gpt-5.6-terra` specialist tracks at exit 0 and the `gpt-5.6-sol` manager at exit 0. The manager identified the publication boundary, fail-open sync, and absolute path leakage as the top risks; those were then hardened. A deliberate missing-vault test failed closed and preserved the previous snapshot hash.

## Canonical source

`[Claude research]\site`

The existing saake.dev hero refinements were preserved. The Brain layer reuses the established token system, Syne/Space Grotesk/Space Mono typography, lime accent, square grid cells, hairline rules, dark/light modes, and existing verification discipline.

notes.relativePath: ReadWrite/03-Infrastructure/HHTech Gateway.md
notes.excerpt: Claude runs through a third-party OpenAI-compatible proxy at hhtechapi.net (sometimes .com), not first-party Anthropic. Configured via ANTHROPICBASEURL + a static bearer key.
notes.body:
# HHTech Gateway

Claude runs through a third-party OpenAI-compatible proxy at `hhtechapi.net` (sometimes `.com`), not first-party Anthropic. Configured via `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` + a static bearer key.

## The key is Opus-only

| Model | Result |
|---|---|
| `claude-opus-5 [1M]` | works (429 = rate limit, retryable) |
| `claude-fable-5`, `claude-sonnet-5`, `claude-haiku-4.5` | **403 — not permitted** |

> [!bug] Still broken on the Mac as of 2026-08-10
> `~/.claude/settings.json` points four model slots at `claude-haiku-4.5`, which 403s. Anything reaching for a small/fast model — background tasks, title generation, some subagents — fails silently. `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` was fixed to Opus; the rest were not. → [[Mac Migration]]

## The health check that lies

`GET /v1/models` returns 200 even while completions are 429ing — it's served by the gateway frontend and stays up while inference refuses work. **Never use it as a recovery probe** (doing so killed 4 healthy chunks). A *tiny* completion lies too: `deepseek-v4-flash` answered a 20-token prompt then failed a real one. Rejections are never billed, so retrying costs only time. → [[Lessons]]

## Phone linking cannot work through it

Architectural, not a missing setting. Phone→desktop resume needs **Anthropic's own relay**, which the gateway doesn't have. The want — "start here, resume from phone" — is achievable via tmux over SSH instead. → [[Oracle Cloud]]

## My wrapper project

A TypeScript CLI + dashboard over the portal and billing API (`claude-workspace/source/hhtech-wrapper/`) that answers "what did usage actually cost and how much balance is left" — which the portal doesn't show cleanly.

```bash
npm run sync | report | reconcile | export | serve | watch
```

**Two data tiers, never confused:** Tier 1 `GET /portal/api/usage` is the authoritative pre-summed aggregate (every headline figure); Tier 2 `GET /portal/api/usage/recent` is a rolling 100-event sample and must never be summed as a total — an early version showed **2 requests** for a day that had **2,751**. Pricing was *calibrated against the live portal* (0.04% agreement on a near-pure Sonnet day), catching a 100× error where the token basis was assumed as 1e8 instead of 1e6. Credentials from `.env` only.

Related: [[Oracle Cloud]] · [[Lessons]]

notes.body:
# Oracle Cloud

Two separate VMs. **Not one.** A `g2g-lol-scout` container was once deployed to the wrong box and had to be migrated off.

| | Home Server | `kali` (instance-20260629-2253) |
|---|---|---|
| IP | `140.238.227.212` | `80.225.254.191` |
| Shape | 2 OCPU / 8 GB (documents claim 4/12, actual is 2/8) | 2 OCPU / 12 GB |
| Role | **Minecraft only** | The workhorse |
| User | `ubuntu` | `ubuntu` |

Both Ubuntu 22.04, ARM Ampere (`VM.Standard.A1.Flex`), region **ap-mumbai-1**.

**Home Server** runs the `minecraft` systemd service (Fabric, port 25565) and nothing else — deploy nothing here. **kali** runs Docker containers `taskmaster-bot`, `discord_bump_bot`, `g2g-lol-scout` ([[G2G Pipeline]]), doubles as a pentest workstation. Mostly idle (load 0.09).

## The actual connection info (found 2026-08-14)

The OCI CLI and API auth were **never in the vault** — they live on the Windows machine and are now referenced here:

| Thing | Where |
|---|---|
| OCI CLI binary | `C:\Program Files (x86)\Oracle\oci_cli\oci.exe` |
| OCI config | `[user home]\.oci\config` (profile `[DEFAULT]`) |
| API private key | `[user home]\.oci\oci_api_key.pem` (+ `.pub`) |
| Full management guide | `[user home]\Downloads\Antigravity Projects\oracle_management_guide.md` |
| Home Server SSH key | `[user home]\Downloads\New folder\Oracle\keys\private.key` |
| kali SSH key | `[user home]\Downloads\New folder\Oracle\Main server Key\ssh-key-2026-06-30.key` (+ `.pub`) |

Identifiers (not secrets — safe to record):

- Tenancy: `ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaaaaaamxbicpgbumy6qhq6ovjrtqljdskjkgrhs27aisfsm7qdru6no6ea`
- User: `ocid1.user.oc1..aaaaaaaaeh2lh3cyq5zy2xaat5pgktavpfthbvjtdpgxp7abx7exlotpi6xa`
- Home Server instance: `ocid1.instance.oc1.ap-mumbai-1.anrg6ljrfrquryic2s3aatl47nxgm3ekdhj2ilnzv6xflry2n5gcgh7didkq`
- Region: `ap-mumbai-1`

Do **not** paste the API private key or SSH key contents into any note. Read them from the paths above.

### Power control (from the guide)

```powershell
# check state
& "C:\Program Files (x86)\Oracle\oci_cli\oci.exe" compute instance get --instance-id "ocid1.instance.oc1.ap-mumbai-1.anrg6ljrfrquryic2s3aatl47nxgm3ekdhj2ilnzv6xflry2n5gcgh7didkq" --query "data.\"lifecycle-state\""
# START / STOP
& "C:\Program Files (x86)\Oracle\oci_cli\oci.exe" compute instance action --instance-id "ocid1.instance.oc1.ap-mumbai-1.anrg6ljrfrquryic2s3aatl47nxgm3ekdhj2ilnzv6xflry2n5gcgh7didkq" --action START|STOP
```

There is also a compiled `MinecraftServerController.exe` with 4 buttons (wake/sleep VM, start/stop Minecraft) wrapping these same calls.

### SSH

```powershell
ssh -i "[user home]\Downloads\New folder\Oracle\keys\private.key" ubuntu@140.238.227.212
```

## The Claude-server plan

Host Claude Code on `kali` so sessions persist and one `~/.claude/` serves Mac, Windows, and phone. **Working tree lives on the server; SSH in and work there** — not an SMB mount (git/npm/ripgrep stat thousands of files and every stat crosses the network).

Tenancy is **Pay As You Go**, which changes the risk model: the 2026-08-18 Always-Free sweep doesn't apply, there's no hard stop (failure mode is a surprise invoice — keep the $1 budget alert), and sleeping only helps at **12 h/day** (1,488 OCPU-hrs vs the 1,500 pool).

**Do not consolidate the two VMs** (rejected): the Ampere allowance is a tenancy-wide pool, so zero compute to win, plus a real risk of one-way downgrade from grandfathered 4/24 to 2/12 and "out of host capacity" on relaunch.

The server is for **persistence, not speed** — the model runs on [[HHTech Gateway]], not the box.

> [!warning] Neither box has Node on the bare host
> `node`/`npm` both "command not found". Docker is how Node runs; any new Node service needs its own Dockerfile.

## Known access gaps

1. **The Minecraft box's documented key may not open it** — only port 25565 responds. Worth fixing independently.
2. **The keys/config are Windows-only.** None of this was in the Mac migration package. → [[Mac Migration]]

Related: [[G2G Pipeline]] · [[Cloudflare and DNS]] · [[Mac Migration]] · [[HHTech Gateway]]

notes.body:
# Transcript and Artifact Archive

All AI-agent history — Claude Code sessions and Antigravity (Claude) conversations — centralized read-only on the Z: drive. Originals also remain at their source locations on C:; the Z: copies are the canonical archive for browsing and mining.

**Why it matters:** sessions are ephemeral, this is not. Every decision, measured number, and trap in this vault was originally worked out in one of these transcripts. When a note says "verified 2026-08-08", the evidence lives here.

## Layout

```
[RaiDrive]/projects\_archive\transcripts\
  claude-code\           88 sessions, ~280 MB, 10 project keys
    <project-key>\
      <session-id>.jsonl              main agent transcript
      <session-id>\                   subagents, tool-results, workflows
      memory\                         per-project memory files
  antigravity\           24 conversations, ~97 MB
    <conversation-uuid>\
      *.md                            artifacts (plans, walkthroughs, task lists)
      task-*\                         per-task artifacts
      .tempmediaStorage\              images pasted/generated mid-conversation
```

## Recovering a conversation

The **compaction summaries** are the fastest way in — dense recaps written when context ran out, appearing inline as `Context compaction` blocks. For a long session, read those before the raw messages. To find a specific discussion, grep the `.jsonl` files for topic terms and rank by hit density rather than reading sequentially. Beware: a session that hit `Prompt is too long` may have died mid-thread and been re-asked in a **fresh session** — the answer lives in the newer, often smaller file.

Subagent runs are never summarised into notes — each keeps its own full transcript under `<session-id>/subagents/`. Transcripts survive on disk even after `/clear` — the file is written as you go, not on exit.

## Source locations (originals, untouched)

| Source | Path | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code transcripts | `[user home]\.claude\projects\` | ~280 MB |
| Antigravity brain | `[user home]\.gemini\antigravity\brain\` | ~97 MB |

- `C--Users-anubh-Downloads-Antigravity-Projects-claude` — 38 sessions, 240 MB. The main workspace: [[saake.dev]], [[HHTech Gateway]], [[Aria AI]], LoveQuest, crypto analysis.
- `C--Users-anubh--claude-supervisor` — 27 sessions for [[Claude Supervisor]].
- `C--Users-anubh-Downloads-Antigravity-Projects-claude-aria-ai` — 9 sessions, 26 MB, [[Aria AI]] fine-tuning.
- `…-g2g-scraper` (2) and `…-league` (1) — [[G2G Pipeline]].

## How to mine it

Grep the `.jsonl` for topic terms and rank by hit density; read compaction summaries (`Context compaction` blocks) before raw messages; a session that died on `Prompt is too long` was usually re-asked in a newer, smaller file — see "Recovering a conversation" above.

notes.body:
# Lessons

Four things learned the hard way, in one place. Each came from a real session — the project note has the full story.

## 1. Recompute, don't trust

Any number that drives a decision gets checked against live data — especially numbers *you* produced. From the crypto analysis: a subagent annualised ATR% as if it were sigma (it isn't — divide by ~1.665); my own RSI-14 used simple averaging instead of Wilder smoothing (31 vs the correct 39.2); two agents quoted different oil prices and a live Binance perp settled it. Training-data prices are stale — the market was ~48% off its peak. → [[Crypto Tax Position]]

## 2. Read the failure mode

One error code means several different things, and the difference decides whether to wait, switch, or stop. A health check that doesn't exercise the path you depend on *lies* — `GET /v1/models` returned 200 while completions were 429ing, and using it as a recovery probe killed four healthy chunks. → [[HHTech Gateway]]

## 3. Measure under real load

Benchmark the thing you'll actually run, at the size you'll actually run it — small samples hid a 2× cost error twice. Windows WDDM doesn't OOM: it pages VRAM to system RAM and training "runs" 100× slower forever, silently. A failure that announces itself is a gift. → [[Aria AI]]

## 4. Fail visible

Never let content visibility depend on a script succeeding. The `.reveal` animation was hidden-by-default, so every JS failure became a blank page. Invert it: the broken state must always land on *visible*. → [[saake.dev]]

Related: [[Aryan (saake)]] · [[Vault Conventions]]

# Vault Conventions

How this vault works. Short on purpose.

## The permission tiers

| Folder | Rule |
|---|---|
| `Private/` | **Never accessed unless Aryan explicitly invites it.** His space — journals, personal life, therapy-style talks. He creates whatever folders he wants in here. |
| `ReadOnly/` | Observe only, never modified. |
| `ReadWrite/` | All working notes live here. |
| Vault root | Only `Home.md` (the map). Nothing else. |

## Writing rules

- **Document as work happens, without asking.** Vault documentation is default behavior, not opt-in (rule set 2026-08-14).
- **Capture feelings, not just facts.** When Aryan talks — especially stream-of-consciousness — take notes on what he says *and* what he means; journal entries go to `Private/Journal/`.
- **Facts get verified dates.** `2026-08-14`, not "last week".
- **Secrets by reference only.** Never paste a key/token/password — record where it lives. This vault may sync.
- **Link liberally.** A wikilink to a note that doesn't exist yet marks a gap. The graph is the point; orphan notes are lost notes.
- **Don't restate the machine-readable.** The vault records what you can't recover from the repo: decisions, numbers, traps, who people are.

## Organization

- **Group by topic in folders.** All saake.dev notes live in `02-Projects/saake.dev/`, not as three siblings with the same prefix. One topic, one folder; one idea, one note inside it.
- **Folders for browsing, links for thinking.** When they disagree, links win.
- **Tags are sparse and functional.** No `moc`/`home` vanity tags. Current set: `profile` `person` `private` `journal` `project` `infra` `method` `reference` `meta` `active` `blocked`.

## Structure

```
Home.md                  the map — start here
Private/                 journals, personal life (hands off unless invited)
  Journal/
ReadOnly/                observe only
ReadWrite/
  01-Profile/            who Aryan is, finances, constraints
  02-Projects/           things being built (topic folders where needed)
  03-Infrastructure/     machines and services underneath
  04-Methods/            lessons that generalise past one project
  05-Reference/          pointers to external evidence
```

# G2G Pipeline

A standing scraper watching G2G's League of Legends account listings for cheap, skin-rich SEA/Singapore accounts, surfacing candidates for manual review. Deployed as the `g2g-lol-scout` container on `kali` ([[Oracle Cloud]]), dashboard at `g2g.saake.dev`.

## What it does

Polls `https://sls.g2g.com/offer/search` (GET, JSON, no auth) with `curl_cffi` + `impersonate="chrome110"` to defeat TLS fingerprinting. Filters: Singapore/SEA only, min 100 skins, max $30. Dedupes new listings against seen ones by `offer_id`.

The one real trap: skin count, champ count, and rank are **not** structured fields — they live inside free-text titles/descriptions in inconsistent per-seller formats. That's why the pipeline has an analysis stage at all.

Design locked 2026-08-08: rule-based parsing (no LLM), Discord alerts via the existing `taskmaster-bot` token, long-lived polling rather than cron.

Related: [[Oracle Cloud]] · [[Cloudflare and DNS]]

notes.body:
# Crypto Tax Position

India tax resident, **paid in crypto as salary** — not as investment profits. Load-bearing for any investment, tax, or currency advice.

## The 30% is not the rate on this income

Section **115BBH** charges income *from the transfer* of a virtual digital asset. Receiving crypto as consideration for services is **not a transfer by the recipient**, so it falls under Salaries (s.17) or PGBP (s.28) at **slab rates**, on INR FMV at the date of receipt.

That FMV then becomes the cost of acquisition under s.115BBH(2)(a) — so converting promptly leaves a near-zero gain for the 30% to bite on.

> [!important] Aryan believed the 30% applied to his whole salary, and was acting on that belief.
> Challenging the user's own stated premise *in his favour* was the single most valuable finding of that session. The reflex to accept a premise because the user asserted it is the failure mode worth naming. → [[Lessons]]

## Two traps that survive the good news

**No VDA cost-basis step-up under s.49.** There is no analogue to s.49(2AA) for sweat equity or s.49(4) for gifts under s.56(2)(x). If an assessing officer asserted nil cost, full proceeds face 30% *on top of* slab tax already paid. Contemporaneous FMV records at each receipt are the only defence.

**s.115BBH allows no loss set-off or carry-forward.** If price falls between receipt and sale, slab tax is owed on the higher receipt FMV and the loss is simply dead. An independent, compliance-neutral reason to convert promptly.

## Currency exposure inverts the standard advice

Income is USD-linked; liabilities are INR. "Indians should hold USD to hedge rupee depreciation" is written for **INR earners** and reverses here — adding USD assets is *concentration*, not a hedge.

As of August 2026: 100% of investable assets (crypto + US equities) USD-linked, 0% INR.

Related: [[Trading Account]] · [[Aryan (saake)]]

notes.body:
# saake.dev

Portfolio site. Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind with the theme **overridden** rather than extended, four self-hosted fonts. Source at `Antigravity Projects/claude/site/` on this machine (paths, stack facts, content model, and the 20 plans: [[Source Layout]]), deployed to Vercel, DNS via [[Cloudflare and DNS]].

## The rebuild deleted rather than corrected

The previous version published claims that were not true — invented statistics, a role at a company that does not exist, a `+1 (555)` placeholder phone number, a promised response time on an address that rejected mail. The rebuild **deleted** them rather than softening them, and the audit became the first case study on the site.

That instinct — when a source is unreliable, remove it rather than patch it — is the same one behind [[Aryan (saake)]]'s name resolution.

## Verification gates

```bash
npm run build && npm run verify   # before any commit
npm run verify:live               # ~90s after push, once Vercel finishes
npm run contrast                  # full colour matrix
```

`scripts/verify.mjs` runs against **built HTML** in `.next/server/app` — not source, not compiled CSS. Eight checks: fabrications, nine banned AI tells, canonicals, no-JS floor, a11y including heading order, share cards as real 1200×630 PNGs, contrast, and a 200 kB gzip ceiling.

> [!tip] The fabrication check excises its own counter-example first
> The flagship case study *quotes* the false claims while describing the audit. So the narrative between `'The previous version of this site claimed'` and `'none had been built.'` is cut before the grep runs. A check whose result moves independently of the property under test is not a diagnostic.

Two traps worth keeping:

- **TELLS greps markup, not CSS.** `border-radius: 20px` inside `globals.css` is legal; a `rounded-2xl` class in JSX is not. That asymmetry is deliberate — it lets the site *depict* a rejected visual system honestly inside an artefact without shipping it as house style.
- **Never hand-write a count into copy.** Four stale claims came from exactly that. Counts are derived via `spelledCount()`. Same habit as [[Lessons]].

`npm run contrast` audits `signal`/`evidence`/`on-accent` alongside the four ink ramps, after a white-on-purple chip at 2.78:1 nearly shipped. Floor is 4.5:1; the tightest surviving pair is 4.51:1.

## Design stance

From `design/system.md` — warm, printed, quiet; the reference is a well-set book, not a dashboard. Nothing decorative survives that is not structural: no radius, no shadow, no gradient, no glow. Every claim checkable, so specificity replaces metrics.

Explicitly rejected — the AI-portfolio signature: dark-mode-plus-neon, purple→pink gradient text, glassmorphism, backdrop-blur cards, animated counters, glow shadows, rounded-2xl everything, floating blurred orbs, "Available for work" pill, monospace-as-body-font. The old site had nine of the ten.

Implementation is twenty plans across five layers in `plans/`.

Related: [[Lessons]] — the entrance animation architecture and the blank-page bug that motivated it.

## Portable workspace archive

Created **2026-08-16** at:

`[user home]\Downloads\saake.dev-workspace-2026-08-16_18-48-52.zip`

- **SHA-256:** `369f07792de80109a3e7af4d23a3d9acf5f529d2b7251dbed63684dce48caad8`
- **Size:** 20,568,982 bytes (~19.6 MiB)
- **Branch:** `checkpoint-hero-refinements`
- **HEAD:** `41c4fdcf5e7b4e775e2ce8535de83aad6002184d`
- Includes complete `.git` history, source, assets, handover/audit documents, and current uncommitted edits.
- Excludes reproducible bulk (`node_modules`, `.next`, caches/build output) and temporary/log files.
- Contains `ARCHIVE-README.txt` and `ARCHIVE-MANIFEST.json` with exact scope and restore steps.
- Verified by ZIP CRC test, full extraction, `git fsck --full`, and byte-for-byte hashes of key changed source files.

Restore: extract `saake.dev-workspace/`, run `npm install`, then `npm run check` and `npm run dev`.

# Mac Migration

Windows → macOS, August 2026. The care package sits at `~/Downloads/Projects/Claude/Claude-Mac-Migration-20260810/`; `~/.claude/` and `~/Projects/` have been restored from it.

## What the move already bought

Aryan's stated reason for wanting a Linux server was that "AI works way better on Linux because of how much more control it has." That was true — **against Windows**. Git-Bash quirks, path mangling, `.ps1` hooks in every hook slot. macOS is genuine Unix: real POSIX paths, zsh, the same tooling.

So the Mac collected most of what the Linux box was for, which is why the [[Oracle Cloud]] Claude-server plan's remaining value is *persistence*, not control.

Oracle Cloud knowledge is now consolidated in one note: [[Oracle Cloud]] (machines, OCI access, and the Claude-server plan).

## Still broken

> [!bug] Model slots that 403
> `~/.claude/settings.json` points `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL`, and `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_4_8_MODEL` at `claude-haiku-4.5`, which the key is not entitled to. `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` was fixed to Opus; these were not. Background tasks and title generation fail silently. → [[HHTech Gateway]]

Also outstanding:

- **Hooks and statusline** were dropped in the restore rather than ported. The Windows config wired all 14 hook events to `claude-supervisor.exe` — see [[Claude Supervisor]] for why that does not port cleanly.
- **The keys never came across.** The export captured `Antigravity Projects\claude\` only, so `oracle_management_guide.md` and the SSH keys — one directory level above — were missed entirely, along with `~/.oci`. This is what blocks the Claude-server plan. → [[Oracle Cloud]]

## Package quirks worth remembering

- **`checksums.sha256` does not exist.** Only `migration_export.py` writes it; this package was built by `migration_pack.py`, which streams source→ZIP and emits no checksums. So `verify.sh` reporting "cannot verify" is expected, not corruption.
- **`cleanup-after-verification.sh` refuses to run** from anywhere outside `~/Migration/`. Deliberate guard — do not loosen it.
- **Project keys changed.** Claude Code derives its project directory name from the cwd, so moved projects get a new key and their history appears under the old one. Relink by **copying** the old key directory to the new name under `~/.claude/projects/`, keeping the original until confirmed.

Related: [[Transcript and Artifact Archive]]

notes.body:
# Aria AI

A persona clone of "Aria (Kaitlyn)" trained on ~33,805 real Telegram messages. Base app at `aria-ai-portable/aria-ai` — ChromaDB RAG, conformance scoring, Flask dashboard on `127.0.0.1:5050`, Telethon listener. Fine-tuning under `finetune/`.

**Goal:** replace the remote [[HHTech Gateway]] drafting path with a fully local QLoRA model on the RTX 3090, keeping the human-approval gate. The motivating risk is privacy — the chat data is ultra-sensitive, and it left the machine on every draft. Both real chat partners consented to the project.

## Two registers, never merged

- `budster` — personal register. Median 4 words, 41.5% single-message response rate.
- `jack` — domme/client register. Median 5 words, dropped apostrophes.

Isolated ChromaDB collections (`aria_budster`, `aria_jack`) over 14,277 conversation pairs.

## Architecture worth keeping

- **`conformance.py`** samples concrete burst lengths and word-count budgets per generation from measured corpus PMFs — the statistical shape is enforced, not hoped for.
- **`chat_engine.py`** generates multiple candidates in parallel and selects the one minimising divergence from Aria's real distributions.
- **RAG top-k is 8, not 25.** Twenty-five drowned the prompt in near-duplicate short texts and pushed the model toward reciting specific past messages.

## Current state (2026-08-07)

Direction locked: **all-local, bigger + curated** — no frontier-API planner, no distillation, export everything first. The two-register split was superseded by a single shared-core run.

`aria_core` — 63,671 train rows pooled across Telegram, Discord and WhatsApp; 1 epoch, batch 4×4, seq 1280, rank 16, preset `balanced`. At step 2,350/3,934 eval_loss was **2.1900 and still improving 9/9 evals**, train 1.8764 — beating budster's best-ever 2.4741 by 0.28. `load_best_model_at_end` is ON, so the final adapter is the best-eval checkpoint.

Deltas were flattening (−0.032 → −0.011), so the remaining steps bought ~0.03–0.05, not another 0.2.

> [!question] The two real ceilings
> **28.1% fact coverage** and **74.5% Kat**. Loss improvements past this point do not move them — they are the open question, not the loss curve.

Related: [[Lessons]] for the 3090 throughput table and the WDDM trap.

research.title: README
research.excerpt: Source for saake.dev.
research.body:
# saake.dev

Source for [saake.dev](https://saake.dev).

The site links here as evidence, so this file describes what is actually in the
repository rather than advertising it.

## Why it was rebuilt

The previous version published claims that were not true — invented statistics,
a role at a company that does not exist, a placeholder phone number beginning
+1 (555), and a promised response time on an address that rejected mail. The
rebuild deleted those rather than correcting them, and the audit is written up
as the first case study on the site.

## Stack

Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind with the theme **overridden** rather
than extended, and four self-hosted font files. Three runtime dependencies:
`next`, `react`, `react-dom`.

Two client components exist — a theme toggle and a single IntersectionObserver
for entrance animations. Everything else is server-rendered. Every page's
content is present in the HTML with JavaScript disabled.

## Layout

```
app/          routes; each declares its own canonical
components/   primitives, shell, the two client components
content/      case studies as typed data — the only place copy lives
scripts/      build-output verification
```

## Verification

```bash
npm run check
```

Builds, then runs `scripts/verify.mjs` against `.next/server/app` — the built
HTML, not the source. It checks:

- **Fabrications.** Greps for the specific false claims the old build carried.
  The flagship case study *quotes* those claims while describing the audit, so
  the narrative is excised before the grep runs. A check whose result moves
  independently of the property under test is not a diagnostic.
- **AI tells.** Nine patterns the design system bans, matched against class
  attributes rather than prose.
- **Canonicals.** Present, unique, self-referential, no trailing slash.
- **No-JS.** Every route server-renders real content and an `<h1>`.
- **Accessibility.** `lang`, skip link, alt text, no click handlers on divs.
- **Contrast.** Recomputed from `app/globals.css` rather than trusted from a
  table. Floor is 4.5:1; the tightest pair is 4.51:1.
- **Weight.** Gzip of the scripts each page actually references.

```bash
npm run contrast
```

Prints every foreground/background ratio in both themes.

## Known limitations

The ~185 kB gzip first load is the React and App Router client runtime. This
site's own client code is under 2 kB. Reducing it further means dropping the
App Router, which has not been done.

## Local development

```bash
npm install
npm run brain:sync
npm run dev
```

The Obsidian-backed control plane lives at `/brain` and is private/local by default. Rebuild its local snapshot with `npm run brain:sync`; `npm run brain:check` refreshes and verifies the full private route set. Normal production builds omit Brain content unless `ENABLE_PRIVATE_BRAIN=1` is set. `npm run brain:sync:public` creates a separate fail-closed snapshot from notes explicitly marked `publish: true` and excludes raw Claude research. Run `npm run brain:upgrade` for a read-only multi-agent pass: three `gpt-5.6-terra` audits in parallel, followed by a `gpt-5.6-sol` manager brief. Generated snapshots and reports are Git-ignored.

## License

MIT for the code. The written content and case studies are not.

# Workspace Agent Directives & Verification Standards

> **Scope:** Applies to any AI assistant, subagent, or autonomous tool operating on this repository and workspace.

## 1. Transparency & Logging Protocol
- **Record All Actions:** Every agent modifying files must maintain clear, verifiable records of modifications, rationale, and verification outputs in relevant project handover notes or logs (`walkthrough.md`, `SAAKEDEV_HANDOVER.md`).
- **Surface File Edits:** Do not execute silent or obscured code modifications; make targeted, clean diffs that are easily auditable.

## 2. Truth & Content Integrity
- **No Hallucinated Claims:** Never fabricate client metrics, corporate logos, business stats, roles, or testimonials.
- **Verifiable Truth Baseline:** All project descriptions, code examples, and technical claims must be grounded in actual source repositories and verifiable architecture.

## 3. Engineering & Design Standards
- **No-JS & Semantic HTML:** All pages must render complete readable content without client-side JavaScript.
- **Accessibility & Contrast:**
  - Maintain WCAG AA compliance (contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 for normal text).
  - Enforce proper heading order (`h1` → `h2` → `h3`) and descriptive accessible labels.
  - Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` on all animations, canvas routines, and WebGL scenes.
- **Performance Budget:** Ensure per-route first-load bundle remains strictly within the defined gzip limits (< 200 kB).

## 4. Verification Gates
Before finishing any slice, run and pass all repository verification gates:
```bash
npm run check
npm run contrast
```

## Brain sync & agent roles

The `/brain` surface is generated from the Obsidian vault plus the Claude research tree.

- Manual refresh: `npm run brain:sync`
- Refresh + build + verify: `npm run brain:check`
- Main management engine: `gpt-5.6-sol` via `custom:hhtechapi.com`
- Bounded sub-agent engine: `gpt-5.6-terra` via `custom:hhtechapi.com`
- Private vault content is excluded by the sync script.
- Notes marked `publish: false` are excluded from the site and counted in the discard ledger.
- Regenerate `content/brain-data.json` after vault or research changes; never edit it by hand.

research.body:
# 📋 MASTER HANDOVER & META-OPTIMIZATION DOSSIER

> **Purpose:** This document is an unvarnished, objective handover briefing for an external AI Agent / Subagents to audit the work done so far, analyze 3,424 raw simulation outputs, and engineer the ultimate deterministic software/steering wrapper around the `kat-ai` model.

---

## 📜 1. Chronological User Prompt Transcript & Project Evolution

Here is the exact record of the user's instructions and design decisions throughout this project:

1. **Identity & Grounding Contract:**
   > *"yeah but like i just want grounding reasoning and understanding for the ai wrapper we made... she's basically a chat indexer who predicts what it might say from a limited understanding... her primary job is to sound exactly like her and she will be 10000% only be selling / be explicit in chats / small talk"*
2. **Store Catalog & Grounding Truth:**
   > User provided the complete store menu: PayPal, Crypto, Throne (`https://throne.com/ariadolly`), Discord Nitro, giftcards. Prices: Short premades ($20/$25), Standard ($30/$35), Long ($55), Customs ($30-$60), Sexting ($30-$60/hr), GF Rent ($20-$40/day), Fansigns ($10-$60), coupon `BUNDLE30`.
3. **Dynamic Intent & Emotional Escalation:**
   > *"intent should be dynamic rather than black or white... dynamic percentage intent so kat ai can be lead towards sexual stuff only if initiated with... shy, very kinky, gets flushed, clingy"*
4. **Scraping Transcripts for Scenario DB:**
   > Scraped 5,164 dialogue scenarios from DirtyTalkDB into SQLite (`dirtytalk_scenarios.db`) to serve as an on-demand RAG kink/phrase bank.
5. **The Reasoning Failure & Over-affection Bug:**
   > Fine-tuned 8B model love-bombed strangers (*"MY BABY IS BACKKKK"*), suggested physical makeup brushes/nail polish, and said *"i don't have my phone / how are you even here"*.
6. **The Dual-Model & Automated Stress-Test Architecture:**
   > User recognized that raw fine-tuning destroys reasoning (catastrophic forgetting) and requested a multi-agent simulation sandbox:
   > - **Tier 1 (Mistral Overseer):** Understands business context, sets strategy, controls lookbacks.
   > - **Tier 2 (Aria Voice):** Generates lowercase raw text.
   > - **Tier 3 (Big Boy Judge - Gemini 3.7 Flash):** Audits accuracy, applies lookback penalties, and mutates prompts toward 80%+ consistency.
7. **The Overnight Breakdown:**
   > 3,424 simulation iterations ran overnight, but Tier 3 (Gemini 3.7 Flash) threw `429 Quota Exceeded` after ~15 turns, causing 98% of runs to execute with a basic fallback evaluator without mutating or improving the software steering wrapper.

---

## 🔍 2. Diagnosis of the Broken Step

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3,424 Raw Simulation Outputs Generated & Saved to Disk                 │
│ (File: simulation_ledger.jsonl)                                        │
└───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ❌ THE BROKEN LINK:                                                    │
│ Tier 3 (Gemini 3.7 Flash) crashed with HTTP 429 Quota Limits on iter 15│
│ Result: 3,400 raw outputs were NEVER systematically audited, and the   │
│ genetic prompt mutation / software steering layer was NEVER generated. │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## 📊 3. Analysis of the 3,424 Raw Outputs (The Dataset)

The 3,424 generated replies in [`simulation_ledger.jsonl`](file:///C:/Users/anubh/Downloads/Antigravity%20Projects/claude/simulation_ledger.jsonl) reveal 4 specific systematic failure patterns:

1. **"Literal Dad" Semantic Confusion:**
   - On ~4% of turns containing the nickname *"dada"*, the model treated it as a biological family member (*"i run this store with my dad"*).
2. **Throne Wishlist Inversion:**
   - On payment questions, Aria asked *"do you want me to look at your wishlist?"* instead of explaining Throne is *her* creator wishlist link.
3. **Lazy Single-Word Deflections:**
   - On complex GF rent or pricing questions, Aria occasionally deflected with *"oki"* or *"idk how to get to my pc 😭"*.
4. **All-Caps Marketing Drift:**
   - On menu inquiries, Aria occasionally shouted in all-caps marketing speech (*"I HAVE PREMADE VIDEOS IN MY STORE 🎉"*) instead of natural lowercase texting.

---

## 🤖 4. Master Meta-Prompt for External Agent / Subagents

Copy and paste the prompt below to your high-IQ agent (Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o / Gemini 1.5 Pro) to orchestrate the parallel optimization bots:

```text
================================================================================
AGENT MISSION: DETERMINISTIC PROMPT-ENGINEERING & SOFTWARE WRAPPER FOR ARIA AI
================================================================================

YOU ARE AN EXPERT CONVERSATIONAL AI ARCHITECT & PROMPT COMPILER.
Your task is to analyze 3,424 raw simulation failure logs from an 18yo NSFW digital creator bot (Aria / @ariadolly) and construct the ultimate deterministic software steering wrapper so she NEVER hallucinates, NEVER breaks character, and converts buyers with 100% catalog accuracy.

INPUT ASSETS AVAILABLE LOCALLY:
1. Store Knowledge Base: server_knowledge_base.json (Full catalog, pricing, Throne link, boundaries)
2. Raw Simulation Ledger: simulation_ledger.jsonl (3,424 generated responses and failure logs)
3. Local Voice Model: kat-ai:latest (Meta Llama 3.1 8B fine-tune on 147k messages)

YOUR OBJECTIVES:
1. PARALLEL FAILURE LOG CLUSTERING:
   - Spin up subagents to parse simulation_ledger.jsonl across all 10 scenario types (Cold Greeting, Menu Inquiry, Budget Haggling, Kinky Audio, Payment, IRL Meet, GF Rent, Discounts, MF3 ID, Flirting).
   - Extract the exact triggers causing:
     a) Literal family/dad hallucinations from "dada"
     b) Throne wishlist direction errors
     c) Lazy one-word deflections ("oki")
     d) Physical makeup/school delusions

2. COMPILE THE DETERMINISTIC SOFTWARE STEERING LAYER:
```

# Real-Time Screen-Watching AI: VERIFIED Cost Breakdown

> [!NOTE]
> All prices below are pulled directly from official source pages, not AI summaries. Sources linked for each.

---

## Sources Used

| Source | URL |
|:---|:---|
| **Alibaba Cloud Model Studio Billing** | [alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/billing-for-model-studio](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/billing-for-model-studio) |
| **Deepgram Pricing** (structured data from page source) | [deepgram.com/pricing](https://deepgram.com/pricing) |
| **Vast.ai GPU Pricing** | [vast.ai/pricing](https://www.vast.ai/pricing) |

---

## 1. Vision Model Pricing (from Alibaba Official Billing Page)

### Qwen3-VL (the dedicated vision models)

**Singapore (International) endpoint — per 1M tokens:**

| Model | Input (≤32K) | Output (≤32K) | Input (32K–128K) | Output (32K–128K) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **qwen3-vl-plus** | **$0.20** | **$1.60** | $0.30 | $2.40 |
| **qwen3-vl-flash** | **$0.05** | **$0.40** | $0.075 | $0.60 |

**China (Beijing) endpoint — per 1M tokens (60-75% cheaper):**

| Model | Input (≤32K) | Output (≤32K) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **qwen3-vl-plus** | **$0.143** | **$1.434** |
| **qwen3-vl-flash** | **$0.022** | **$0.215** |

### Qwen3.7-Max (current flagship, with native vision)

**Singapore (International) — per 1M tokens:**

| Model | Input | Output |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **qwen3.7-max** | **$2.50** (list, 50% off promo) | **$7.50** (list, 50% off promo) |

**China (Beijing) — per 1M tokens:**

| Model | Input | Output |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **qwen3.7-max** | **$1.65** (list, 50% off promo) | **$4.951** (list, 50% off promo) |

### Qwen Omni (vision + audio native, for real-time screen + voice)

**Singapore (International) — per 1M tokens:**

| Model | Input (text/image/video) | Input (audio) | Output (text) | Output (text+audio) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **qwen3.5-omni-plus** | **$1.40** | $11.00 | $8.30 | $44.00 |
| **qwen3.5-omni-flash** | **$0.40** | $3.00 | $2.20 | $11.90 |
| **qwen3.5-omni-plus-realtime** | **$2.10** | $16.50 | $12.40 | $62.00 |
| **qwen3.5-omni-flash-realtime** | **$0.55** | $4.50 | $3.30 | $17.70 |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Qwen Omni Realtime models handle BOTH vision and voice natively** — this could replace your need for a separate voice API entirely. But output audio tokens are **extremely expensive** ($17–$62/M tokens).

---

## 2. Deepgram Voice Agent Pricing (from page source structured data)

**Per minute of voice agent conversation:**

| Plan | Standard Agent | Custom (BYO LLM) | Advanced Agent |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Pay As You Go** | **$0.056/min** | **$0.050/min** | **$0.122/min** |
| **Growth** | **$0.051/min** | **$0.041/min** | **$0.110/min** |

**Per hour (calculated):**

| Plan | Standard | Custom (BYO LLM) | Advanced |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **PAYG** | **$3.36/hr** | **$3.00/hr** | **$7.32/hr** |
| **Growth** | **$3.06/hr** | **$2.46/hr** | **$6.60/hr** |

**Deepgram STT only** (if building your own pipeline):
- Flux Streaming English: **$0.0065/min** = **$0.39/hr**
- Nova-3 Streaming: **$0.0048/min** = **$0.29/hr**

**Deepgram TTS only**:
- Aura-2: **$0.030/1K chars**
- Flux TTS: **$0.045/1K chars**

---

## 3. Hourly Cost Estimates for Screen Watching

### Token math for screenshots
- A 1080p screenshot ≈ 1,000–3,000 tokens (depends on model's image tokenization)
- With change-detection (only send when screen changes): ~6 frames/min = 360 frames/hr

### Vision-only API cost per hour

| Capture Rate | Frames/hr | ~Tokens/hr | qwen3-vl-flash ($0.05/M in) | qwen3-vl-plus ($0.20/M in) | qwen3.7-max ($2.50/M in) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Change-detect (~6/min) | 360 | ~540K | **$0.03** | **$0.11** | **$1.35** |
| Every 5 sec | 720 | ~1.1M | **$0.06** | **$0.22** | **$2.75** |
| Every 2 sec | 1,800 | ~2.7M | **$0.14** | **$0.54** | **$6.75** |
| 1 FPS | 3,600 | ~5.4M | **$0.27** | **$1.08** | **$13.50** |

*Plus output tokens — add ~10-30% on top for model responses.*

### Combined: Vision + Voice per hour

| Setup | Vision/hr | Voice/hr | **Total/hr** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Budget**: qwen3-vl-flash + Deepgram Standard | ~$0.05 | ~$3.36 | **~$3.41** |
| **Mid**: qwen3-vl-plus + Deepgram Standard | ~$0.15 | ~$3.36 | **~$3.51** |
| **Flagship**: qwen3.7-max + Deepgram Advanced | ~$2.00 | ~$7.32 | **~$9.32** |
| **All-in-one**: qwen3.5-omni-flash-realtime | ~$3–$8 combined (depends on audio volume) | included | **~$3–$8** |

---

## 4. Self-Hosted GPU Costs

From Vast.ai (live marketplace, prices vary by supply/demand):

| GPU | Typical On-Demand | Qwen Model It Runs |
|:---|:---|:---|
| RTX 4090 (24GB) | ~$0.30–$0.80/hr | Qwen3-VL 7B quantized |
| L40S (48GB) | ~$0.80–$1.50/hr | Qwen3-VL 32B |
| A100 80GB | ~$1.50–$3.00/hr | Qwen3-VL 72B |
| 4×H100 cluster | ~$8–$16/hr | Full flagship (impractical) |

> [!WARNING]
> GPU marketplace prices fluctuate. Check [vast.ai/pricing](https://www.vast.ai/pricing) for live rates. The numbers above are typical ranges, not fixed quotes.

### When self-hosting wins

Self-hosting is cheaper when your **hourly token bill exceeds the GPU rental cost**. At qwen3-vl-flash prices ($0.05/M), the API is so cheap that self-hosting rarely makes sense unless you're doing 24/7 1-FPS capture at scale.

Self-hosting makes sense for:
- **Privacy** (screen data never leaves your machine)
- **Qwen3.7-max-level quality** without $2.50/M token costs
- **24/7 always-on** monitoring

---

## 5. Honest Corrections From My Previous Analysis

| What I said before | What the real data shows |
|:---|:---|
| "Qwen3.8-Max" exists | **No such model on the billing page.** The actual latest flagship is **qwen3.7-max** (released May/June 2026). The search summary hallucinated "3.8-Max". |
| Qwen3-VL Plus at $0.20/M input | ✅ **Confirmed** — exactly $0.20/M input (Singapore) |
| qwen3.7-max at $2/$6 per M tokens | **Close but not exact.** Real price: **$2.50 input / $7.50 output** (Singapore), currently 50% off promo |
| Voice AI ~$4–$8/hr | ✅ **Confirmed** — Deepgram Standard Agent is $3.36/hr PAYG, Advanced is $7.32/hr |
| GPU rental $0.50–$1.50/hr for a 4090 | ✅ **Ballpark correct** — Vast.ai shows ~$0.30–$0.80 for 4090s |

> [!CAUTION]
> The "Qwen3.8-Max (2.4T parameter)" model from my earlier analysis came from **web search summaries that may be fabricated or conflated**. The official Alibaba billing page as of August 2026 lists **qwen3.7-max** as the top-tier model. Always verify against [the official billing docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/billing-for-model-studio).

# saake.dev — Gemini / Antigravity Handover

> **Purpose:** This is the starting context for continuing work on `saake.dev` in Antigravity IDE with Gemini. Read this file first, then inspect the repository and the manifests beside it. Do not treat historical claims as current truth without checking the code, git state, and live site.

## 0. Immediate instruction to the next agent

You are taking over an existing portfolio project, not starting a generic template. Before changing code:

1. Read this handover completely.
2. Read `handover/project-file-manifest.json` and `handover/transcript-manifest.json`.
3. Inspect the current working tree and the full diff; **preserve existing uncommitted work unless the user explicitly asks to discard it**.
4. Run the existing verification commands before making design decisions:

```bash
npm install
npm run check
npm run contrast
```

5. Start by producing a short, evidence-based audit of what is currently real, what is incomplete, and what the next smallest high-value improvement is. Do not invent biography, client work, metrics, roles, testimonials, or technical claims.

## 1. Project identity and desired outcome

- Brand/domain: **saake.dev** / Saake.
- User identity: Aryan; online handle `saake`; GitHub `https://github.com/RealSaake`.
- Desired positioning: a premium-studio-style personal portfolio that demonstrates taste, design thinking, creative development, and technical craft through the site itself.
- The user explicitly rejected the generic “AI portfolio” look. The site should feel authored, specific, expressive, and human.
- The earlier creative reference direction came from studying PandaX Studio and Karakal work. Use them as visual research references, not as material to copy one-for-one or misrepresent as the user's work.
- The site must be truthful. The old site contained fabricated claims; the rebuild intentionally removed them rather than polishing them.

## 2. Current repository state (verified from disk)

### Git

- Branch: `master`, tracking `origin/master`.
- Last committed HEAD: `9e0d678` — `Let the layout reflow instead of clipping it`.
- The working tree is **not clean**. At the original handover generation, modified tracked files included; later Gemini work is recorded in section 2A:

- Untracked additions include `components/hero-scene-loader.tsx`, `components/hero-scene.tsx`, `components/waveline-visualizer.tsx`, and `public/media/`.
- Do not reset or overwrite this work without first reviewing it.
