research.body:
# 4.4 — About and contact

**Layer:** 4 — Pages · **Depends on:** 2.4, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1 · **Blocks:** 5.1, 5.4

---

## Objective

Two pages, both short. `/about` is the humanize beat; `/contact` is the ask.

These are the two pages where a thin track record is most tempting to pad, and the two where padding is most expensive. Everything else on the site can hide behind an artifact — a case study is judged on the work it describes. An about page is judged on nothing but the writing, and a contact page is checked, not read: a visitor who reaches it is deciding whether to spend a message, and every unverifiable detail on it is a reason not to.

So the governing constraint for both pages is subtraction. The old versions contained a phone number, a city, a response-time promise, working hours, an availability pill, a dead newsletter button, and six social links — and not one of those was true. The replacements are shorter, and shorter is the point.

---

## Prerequisites

- 2.4 shipped — shell, nav, footer, skip link, focus management.
- 2.1 and 2.3 shipped — `Rule`, `Label`, `SectionHead`, `Prose`, `ExternalLink`; `Button`/`ButtonLink`, `SpecTable`.
- 3.1 complete — everything in "What was deleted" below is gone from the tree.
- 3.4 complete — the pronoun partition and jargon gradient are defined; this page's prose obeys them.
- **3.3 questions 1–5 answered.** These two pages are the only ones in the build that cannot ship with a placeholder. A case study can omit a detail; a contact page cannot omit its channel, and an about page cannot omit its subject.

### What was deleted, and does not come back

| Deleted | Why it cannot return |
|---|---|
| `+1 (555) 123-4567` | Invented. `555-123-4567` is the canonical fake-phone-number pattern in North American film and television — a reader who recognises it stops trusting the page, and many will. |
| `San Francisco, CA` | Invented location. |
| "I typically respond to emails within 24 hours during business days" | A promise to a stranger, unenforceable, and pointless: nobody declines to write because the reply might take two days. |
| Stated working hours | Implies an operation that does not exist. |
| "Subscribe to Newsletter" button | Non-functional. There is no newsletter. |
| Instagram, YouTube, Dev.to, Medium, Stack Overflow, CodePen under generic `saake` slugs | Unverified. Six links, six chances to be wrong. |
| "Available for work" status pill | Availability changes; the page does not. A stale pill is worse than none. |

### The rule these share

**An unconfirmed profile ships as nothing, not as a link.**

The asymmetry is stark. Adding a verified profile later costs one line of JSX. A dead link on the contact page is a broken promise on the most-scrutinised page of the site, discovered by exactly the person you most wanted to reach — and it is discovered *by them clicking*, which means the failure is attributed to you at the moment of highest intent.

**Confirmed:** `github.com/RealSaake` is correct and public — it ships.
**Wrong, deleted:** `github.com/saake` (a different account).

### Blocking unknowns — route to 3.3, never guess

| Unknown | State |
|---|---|
| How to credit the user | GitHub profile `name` reads `anubhav aryan`; `saake-engine.json` says `Sake`; `skills.ts` says `Saake`. The name is known; the **preference** is not. 3.3 Q1. |
| Whether "Ari" is real | Files disagree. 3.3 Q2. |
| LinkedIn URL | `linkedin.com/in/saake` unverified. 3.3 Q3. |
| Does `hello@saake.dev` receive mail | **Resolved — it does not exist.** Cloudflare Email Routing is live on the zone (`status: ready`) with nine literal rules, and `hello@` is not among them. **`hi@saake.dev` → `saakedev@gmail.com`, enabled and verified.** That is the contact address. Also live: `aria@` and `oneprompt@` → same inbox; `kat@` → a different one. The catch-all rule exists but is **disabled**, so anything not explicitly routed is rejected — which is why `hello@` would have silently failed. |
| Twitter/X | Unverified. 3.3 Q5. |

**Do not invent a single biographical fact to fill a gap.** If an answer is missing at build time, the section containing it is omitted, not approximated. A page with three sections and no lies is finishable; a page with five sections and two guesses is not fixable, because nobody will remember which two.

---

## Page order law

P17 — value precedes ask. The spine is **Position → Demonstrate → Prove → Humanize → Qualify → Corroborate → Ask.**

`/about` is **Humanize**. It sits *after* the proof, both in the nav order and in the reader's path. This inverts the templated pattern where About is the second nav item and the first thing anyone reads — an arrangement that asks for trust before offering evidence.

`/contact` is **Ask**, and comes last in the nav.

The practical test for anything proposed for either page: *does this ask before it gives?* An availability pill asks. A newsletter signup asks. A response-time promise pretends to give and actually asks — it requests that the reader treat a claim as a commitment.

---

## The about page's real job

With a short track record, the instinct is to inflate. The instinct is wrong, and not for moral reasons — for structural ones.

The about page sits directly downstream of the flagship case study (4.3), which is a careful, specific, self-critical argument about why fabrication is self-defeating. A padded bio placed after that page **refutes the page**. The reader has just been told that inflation spends credibility; the next screen inflates. It is the identical failure mode 3.3 found in the repos — careful work undermined by its own surrounding copy.

Whereas a short honest about page after a strong case study reads as confidence. The case study already did the arguing. The about page only has to be true.

**What it should contain:** what the person is working on now, how they think about the work, and what they are trying to get better at. Stated specifically, in the voice 3.4 defines.

**What it must not contain:** years of experience, a count of projects, technology "levels," a percentage, a self-assessment score, a client count, or any number that cannot be pointed at. The old `data/skills.ts` had roughly 96 such numbers and a `hackermanQuotient` of 89. Zero of them were measurements.

**Under-claiming is the safer error.** A reader who finishes the about page thinking *this person is early but serious* has received the true signal and is the reader worth having. A reader who thinks *this person claims more than the work shows* is lost, and cannot be recovered by anything later on the page.

---

## Steps

### Step 1 — `/about`

**Route:** `app/about/page.tsx` · **Server component. No `"use client"`.**

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [nav — shell from 2.4]                          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                  │
│  ABOUT                          ← Label, mono    │
│                                                  │
│  A two-line statement in display                 │
│  serif. Noun phrase, no verb.       ← §1         │
│                                                  │
│  ────────────────────────────────   ← Rule       │
│                                                  │
│  Two or three paragraphs. Prose      ← §2        │
│  measure, 65ch. What the work is,                │
│  how it's approached. First person               │
│  throughout — this is a response                 │
│  field in 3.4's partition.                       │
│                                                  │
│  ────────────────────────────────                │
│                                                  │
│  NOW                                 ← §3        │
│  Three or four lines. Present tense.             │
│  Dated. Deletable.                               │
│                                                  │
│  ────────────────────────────────                │
│                                                  │
│  TOOLS                               ← §4        │
│  SpecTable — flat list, no levels.               │
│                                                  │
│  ────────────────────────────────                │
│                                                  │
│  → Read the rebuild case study      ← §5         │
│  → Contact                                       │
│                                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  [footer]                                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| § | Purpose | Enacts | Components | Content from |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Position the person, not the work | P15 tagline frame, P5 label register | `Label`, `SectionHead` | 3.4 · needs Q1 |
| 2 | How the work is approached | P12 pronoun partition (response register), P13 gradient — low jargon here | `Prose` | 3.4 |
| 3 | Current state, honestly dated | P14 specificity replaces metrics, P20 deliberate absence | `Prose`, `Label` | 3.3 |
| 4 | Tools, as inventory not credential | P16 one argues / rest inventory | `SpecTable`, `Label` | verified from repos |
| 5 | Route onward, don't dead-end | P17, P18 | `ButtonLink`, `ExternalLink` | — |

**§1 — the statement.** P15's frame: noun phrases, zero finite verbs, generic first half, all specificity in the object. Fails if it contains "I am a…" — that is a finite verb and a self-description, and it reads as a résumé header. Cannot be drafted until Q1 resolves how the user is credited.

**§2 — the paragraphs.** First person throughout; this is a response field. The constraint from 3.4 that matters most here: no sentence may begin *"I realised that users needed…"* — the partition forbids blending, and that construction is self-congratulation about having noticed something. Two paragraphs is enough. Three is the maximum. Jargon density near 0% — the technical register belongs in the case studies, not here.

**§3 — Now.** Present tense, four lines maximum, and written to be deleted. The value is that it is current; a "Now" section last updated eleven months ago is worse than no section, because it is dated evidence of neglect. Include the date it was last edited, in the label register. If nobody will update it, cut the section — P20.

**§4 — Tools.** A flat alphabetical list rendered through `SpecTable`. No proficiency levels, no years, no project counts, no ordering by skill. This is the direct replacement for the 32-skill table with ~96 invented numbers, and the replacement is deliberately less impressive-looking. Include only what appears in a verified `package.json` or source file from 3.3. TypeScript, React, Next.js, Tailwind, Firebase, Python are all supportable. Anything else needs a file behind it.

**§5 — Onward links.** The about page is the humanize beat, so it hands off rather than closing: one link into the flagship case study, one to contact. `github.com/RealSaake` also appears here via `ExternalLink` — P18, send them somewhere you don't control. Note the 3.3 consequence: linking the profile publishes its READMEs, so the featured repos' READMEs must be cleaned before this link ships.

**Metadata:**

```tsx
// app/about/page.tsx
import type { Metadata } from "next";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "About",
  description: "",           // ← one sentence, no superlatives. Needs Q1.
  alternates: { canonical: "/about" },
  openGraph: {
    title: "About",
    description: "",         // ← must match `description` exactly
    url: "/about",
    type: "profile",
  },
};
```

`metadataBase` is set once in the root layout (5.2), so `canonical: "/about"` resolves absolute. The literal string must be `"/about"` — not `""`, not the homepage. Canonicalising subpages to the root is the exact defect 5.2 exists to prevent.

**No JSON-LD `Person` node on this page until Q1 resolves.** Structured data is a machine-readable fabrication surface: a

research.body:
# 1.4 — Fonts and CI guardrails

**Layer:** 1 — Foundation · **Depends on:** 1.2, 1.3 · **Blocks:** 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4

---

## Objective

Two deliverables that look unrelated and are not.

1. **Three self-hosted typefaces**, loaded with zero layout shift and zero third-party requests.
2. **CI that fails the build** when a component reaches outside the token layer 1.3 established.

They belong in one plan because they are the same problem: a design system is only a system if it is enforced. 1.3 wrote the tokens; nothing yet prevents a developer — or a code generator — from typing `text-blue-500`, `p-7`, or `#fff` and shipping it. The tokens are a suggestion until CI makes them a constraint.

The typefaces are the other half of the same enforcement. Three faces, each with exactly one job, is a decision that only holds if the fourth face is impossible to add casually. Fonts loaded from a CDN, or via `<link>` to Google Fonts, are one line away from becoming four faces and a third-party dependency on every page load.

**The specific tell being designed against:** the user's stated objection is that AI-generated sites look "very ugly and very AI like." Inter loaded from Google Fonts on a white background with `rounded-lg` cards is the visual signature of that entire category. `design/system.md` rejects Inter explicitly. This plan is what stops it coming back.

---

## Prerequisites

- 1.2 complete — clean Next.js 14 App Router tree, git initialised, `package.json` present.
- 1.3 complete — `styles/tokens/*.css`, `app/globals.css`, `tailwind.config.ts` with the theme **overridden, not extended**, and `scripts/verify-tokens.mjs` passing.
- Node available. **Python is not installed on this machine** — every script here is Node.
- Git Bash. Windows path separators in config files must be forward slashes; `glob` patterns in ESLint and Stylelint configs are POSIX regardless of platform.

### Resolved ambiguity 1 — the three faces are available and self-hostable

Verified against the Fontsource API this session:

| Face | Role | Weights available | Styles | Subsets | Licence | Variable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Instrument Serif** | Display only | **400 only** | normal, italic | latin, latin-ext | OFL-1.1 | No |
| **Geist Sans** | Body, UI | 100–900 (9 static) | normal | latin | OFL-1.1 | No |
| **Geist Mono** | Label register only | 100–900 | normal, italic | latin, latin-ext, cyrillic, cyrillic-ext, vietnamese, symbols2 | OFL-1.1 | **Yes** |

All three are OFL-1.1. Self-hosting is permitted, including in a commercial context, with no attribution requirement in the rendered page. The licence must ship in the repo alongside the font files.

**Instrument Serif has exactly one weight: 400.** This is a hard constraint on the design system, not an inconvenience, and it needs stating plainly because it will otherwise be discovered halfway through building 4.3.

Consequences:
- There is no bold display serif. A heading that needs more weight gets more *size*, or the label register above it, or a rule beneath it — never `font-weight: 700`.
- **Never apply `font-weight` above 400 to a display element.** The browser will synthesise a fake bold by smearing the outline, and synthetic bold on a high-contrast serif is one of the ugliest artifacts in web typography. It looks exactly like the "AI-like" register the site is avoiding.
- Italic exists at 400 and is available for editorial emphasis in prose.

This is a feature. One weight forces hierarchy to come from scale and spacing, which is what `design/system.md` §2 already specifies with its eight-step 1.25 ratio.

### Resolved ambiguity 2 — weights to actually ship

Do not ship 9 weights of anything. Every weight is a separate file on the critical path.

| File | Weight | Style | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instrument Serif | 400 | normal | `--t-display`, `--t-h1`, `--t-h2`, `--t-h3` |
| Instrument Serif | 400 | italic | editorial emphasis in `Prose` |
| Geist Sans | 400 | normal | body, `--t-body`, `--t-body-s`, `--t-lead` |
| Geist Sans | 500 | normal | UI elements, buttons, nav |
| Geist Mono | 400 | normal | the label register only — `--t-label` |

**Five files.** Geist Mono is variable, but a variable font carrying 100–900 plus six subsets is larger than one static 400 latin cut when only 400 latin is used. Take the static cut and subset it.

Geist Sans 500 is the only concession to a second weight, and it earns it: the label register is mono, so sans-serif emphasis in nav and buttons has nowhere else to come from. If 500 turns out unused after 2.4 ships, delete it.

---

## Steps

### Step 1 — Acquire and place the files

`next/font/local` requires the files in the repo. Do not use `next/font/google` — it fetches at build time and, more importantly, it makes adding a fourth Google-hosted face a one-line change.

```
public/fonts/
  instrument-serif-400-normal.woff2
  instrument-serif-400-italic.woff2
  geist-sans-400-normal.woff2
  geist-sans-500-normal.woff2
  geist-mono-400-normal.woff2
  OFL.txt                          ← licence, all three faces
```

woff2 only. woff and ttf fallbacks are dead weight — woff2 has had universal support across every browser in the 5.3 matrix for years, and a browser old enough to need woff will fail on `clamp()` in the type scale anyway.

Source the files from Fontsource (`npm i @fontsource/instrument-serif @fontsource/geist-sans @fontsource/geist-mono`, copy the woff2 files out of `node_modules`, then uninstall) or download the release archives directly. **Do not leave the Fontsource packages as dependencies** — they add CSS that competes with the `next/font/local` declarations and will produce duplicate `@font-face` rules.

Subset to latin. Everything the site renders is English; latin-ext, cyrillic, and vietnamese are unused bytes on the critical path.

### Step 2 — Declare the faces with metric-compatible fallbacks

**File: `app/fonts.ts`**

```ts
import localFont from "next/font/local";

export const displaySerif = localFont({
  src: [
    { path: "../public/fonts/instrument-serif-400-normal.woff2", weight: "400", style: "normal" },
    { path: "../public/fonts/instrument-serif-400-italic.woff2", weight: "400", style: "italic" },
  ],
  variable: "--font-display",
  display: "swap",
  preload: true,
  fallback: ["Georgia", "Times New Roman", "serif"],
  adjustFontFallback: "Times New Roman",
});

export const bodySans = localFont({
  src: [
    { path: "../public/fonts/geist-sans-400-normal.woff2", weight: "400", style: "normal" },
    { path: "../public/fonts/geist-sans-500-normal.woff2", weight: "500", style: "normal" },
  ],
  variable: "--font-body",
  display: "swap",
  preload: true,
  fallback: ["-apple-system", "BlinkMacSystemFont", "Segoe UI", "Helvetica Neue", "Arial", "sans-serif"],
  adjustFontFallback: "Arial",
});

export const labelMono = localFont({
  src: [{ path: "../public/fonts/geist-mono-400-normal.woff2", weight: "400", style: "normal" }],
  variable: "--font-mono",
  display: "swap",
  preload: false,   // ← label register only; not needed for first paint
  fallback: ["ui-monospace", "SFMono-Regular", "Menlo", "Consolas", "monospace"],
  adjustFontFallback: "Arial",
});
```

Three decisions worth the explanation, because each is a place the default is wrong:

**`display: "swap"`, not `"optional"` or `"block"`.** `block` gives invisible text for up to 3 seconds — a blank page on a slow connection. `optional` may never load the font at all on a slow first visit, meaning the site's typography, which is most of its visual identity, silently doesn't happen. `swap` shows fallback text immediately and swaps when ready. The swap causes reflow unless the metrics match, which is what the next decision handles.

**`adjustFontFallback`** is the mechanism that keeps CLS at zero. Next.js computes `size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, `descent-override`, and `line-gap-override` on the fallback face so the fallback occupies the same vertical space as the real font. Without it, `swap` guarantees a visible layout shift on every first load — and CLS is one of the three Core Web Vitals 5.2 is targeting.

**`preload: false` on the mono.** It is used only for `--t-label` — small uppercase labels. Preloading three faces means three high-priority requests competing on the critical path. The labels can swap in a frame late; the body and display cannot.

`variable` exposes each as a CSS custom property, which is how `tailwind.config.ts` consumes them. This is the seam between this plan and 1.3.

### Step 3 — Wire into the root layout and Tailwind

**In `app/layout.tsx`** — the class names go on `<html>` so the variables are available to everything, including portalled content:

```tsx
import { displaySerif, bodySans, labelMono } from "./fonts";

// on <html>:
className={`${displaySerif.variable} ${bodySans.variable} ${labelMono.variable}`}
```

**In `tailwind.config.ts`** — the `fontFamily` key is **overridden, not extended**, consistent with 1.3's treatment of the rest of the theme:

```ts
fontFamily: {
  display: ["var(--font-display)", "Georgia", "serif"],
  body:    ["var(--font-body)", "system-ui", "sans-serif"],
  mono:    ["var(--font-mono)", "ui-monospace", "monospace"],
},
```

Overriding rather than extending is what makes `font-sans` and `font-serif` fail to compile. There are exactly three families and they are named for their roles. A developer who wants a fourth has to edit this file, which is a visible diff in review rather than an invisible utility class in a component.

**Base element defaults in `app/globals.css`** — set once so components never declare a family:

```css
body { font-family: theme(fontFamily.body); }
h1, h2, h3, .display { font-family: theme(fontFamily.display); font-weight: 400; }
.label { font-family: theme(fontFamily.mono); }
```

The explicit `font-weight: 400` on display elements is load-bearing, not redundant. Browser stylesheets set `h1`–`h3` to `bold`. Without this line every heading on the site renders in synthesised fake bold — the exact artifact Step 0 warned about, applied to every heading, invisible to anyone who has not seen the real face.

### Step 4 — Stylelint: no raw values in CSS

```bash
npm i -D stylelint stylelint-config-standard
```

**File: `.stylelintrc.json`**

```json
{
  "extends": ["stylelint-config-standard"],
  "rules": {
    "color-no-hex": true,
    "declaration-property-value-disallowed-list": {
      "/^font-family$/": ["/Inter/", "/Roboto/", "/Open Sans/", "/Poppins/", "/Montserrat/"],
      "/^box-shadow$/": ["/.+/"],
      "/^border-radius$/": ["/^(?!0).+/"]
    },
    "function-disallowed-list": ["rgb", "rgba", "hsl", "hsla"],
    "custom-property-pattern": "^(font-|t-|s-|dur-|ease-|reveal-|band-|paper|surface|rule|rule-strong|muted|muted-2|ink|ink-2|a-[1-6]|accent|focus|grain).*$"
  },
  "ignoreFiles": ["styles/tokens/*.css", "**/*.min.css", ".next/**"]
}
```

`ignoreFiles` on `styles/tokens/*.css` is essential and slightly counterintuitive: the token files are the *only* place raw hex values are legal. They are where colour is defined. Everywhere else, a hex literal means someone bypassed the system.

The `font-family` blocklist names the five faces that signal templated design. This is a deliberately opinionated rule and the reason for it is the user's brief, not a technical concern.

`box-shadow` is disallowed entirely — `design/system.md` §5 has no shadow token, because elevation comes from the edge, not from a blur (P1). `border-radius` is disallowed at any non-zero value; the system's radius is 0 with **one** documented exception, the status dot, which is handled in Step 6.

### Step 5 — ESLint: no off-token utilities in components

```bash
npm i -D eslint-plugin-tailwindcss
```

Add to the ESLint config:

```js
{
  plugins: ["tailwindcss"],
  rules: {
    "tailwindcss/no-custom-classname": ["error", {
      whitelist: ["label", "display", "prose", "mortar", "lift", "section", "section-band", "grain", "js", "sr-on

research.body:
# 3.3 — Project ground truth

**Layer:** 3 — Content · **Depends on:** 3.1 · **Blocks:** 3.2, 3.4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4

---

## Objective

Establish what each real project actually does, verified against source code and live deployments rather than against its own README.

This plan exists because of a finding that changes the shape of the whole content layer: **the fabrication is not confined to the portfolio site.** The same inflation pattern appears in the READMEs of the projects the portfolio was supposed to describe. Plan 3.1 deletes invented claims from `saake.dev`. If 3.3 then sources replacement copy from the project READMEs, the fabrication survives the purge — laundered through a second document.

So the rule for this plan is narrower than "find out what the projects do":

> **The code is the source of truth. The README is a claim about the code and is treated as unverified until read against it.**

Every sentence that reaches the site must trace to a file, a route, a dependency, a response header, or a rendered screen. Not to a status report.

---

## Prerequisites

- 3.1 complete — the fabrication inventory is written and its dispositions (DELETE / FIX / HOLD) are known.
- Read access to `github.com/RealSaake` (public; no auth required).
- `curl` and `node`. Python is not installed on this machine — do not write Python verification scripts.
- The five blocking unknowns from `plans/README.md`. Three are resolved below. Two are not, and cannot be resolved without the user.

### Resolved ambiguity 1 — the identity conflict has a third data point

3.1 recorded a conflict it could not settle: `data/saake-engine.json` says `legal_name: "Sake"` (one 'a'); `data/skills.ts` says `"Saake"` (two). Neither is a name.

The GitHub profile's `name` field, which neither repo file reflects, reads **`anubhav aryan`**. Three independent corroborations:

| Evidence | Value | How obtained |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub profile `name` | `anubhav aryan` | `GET api.github.com/users/RealSaake` |
| Repo created 2022-03-02 | `RealSaake/anubhavaryan` | repo listing |
| That repo's `CNAME` | `anubhavaryan.com` | raw fetch — a domain someone registers for their own name |
| Local OS account | `anubh` | working directory path |

`anubhavaryan.com` does **not** resolve (curl exit 000, no DNS). The domain in the CNAME was either never bought or has lapsed.

**Disposition: still HOLD, but for a different reason.** The name is now known with reasonable confidence. What is not known is *how the user wants to be credited* — legal name, the `Saake` handle, or both. That is a preference, not a fact, and P12/P15 make it load-bearing: the tagline frame needs a credentialed subject, and the about page needs a byline. Ask; do not choose.

Do **not** ship `Sake`. It matches no evidence, and `sake.dev` does not resolve while `saake.dev` does.

### Resolved ambiguity 2 — "Ari"

`data/skills.ts` lists aliases `["Saake", "Ari"]`; `saake-engine.json` lists `["Saake"]`. Given `anubhav aryan`, `Ari` is a plausible contraction of the surname. Plausible is not verified. **HOLD** — one question to the user, and it ships as nothing until answered.

### Resolved ambiguity 3 — repo inventory

16 public repos, of which 1 is a fork (`copyparty`, not own work) and 4 are empty 0 KB shells (`saake.dev`, `aicluster`, `Portfolio`, `saake`). Eleven repos contain code. Account created 2019-07-22.

---

## Steps

### Step 1 — Establish the verification ladder

Every claim about a project gets a tier. The tier determines whether it may appear on the site and in what register.

| Tier | Meaning | May appear on site |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Executed** | Verified by running it, or by a response from a live deployment | Yes, as a plain statement |
| **B — In source** | The code that implements it was read | Yes, as a plain statement |
| **C — Declared** | A README or config asserts it; not contradicted by source | Only hedged, or not at all |
| **D — Contradicted** | Source contradicts the claim | Never. Route to 3.1 for deletion |
| **E — Unverifiable** | Requires hardware, credentials, or history not in the repo | Never as a capability claim |

Tier C is where fabrication enters. A README bullet nobody has traced to code is not evidence — it is the *same category of artifact* as `hackermanQuotient: 89`. Someone wrote a number they liked.

### Step 2 — waveline · Tier A/B verified

**Repo:** `RealSaake/waveline` · TypeScript · created 2025-07-25, last push 2025-07-26 · 302 KB · 28 source files
**Live:** `https://waveline.vercel.app` → 200 · `/live` → 200

Next.js App Router. Dependencies: `next`, `react`, `react-dom`, `konva`, `react-konva`, `framer-motion`, `colorthief`, `html2canvas`, `jose`, `clsx`, `@vercel/speed-insights`.

**Tier B — read in source:**

| Capability | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Spotify OAuth, server-side | `api/spotify-auth`, `api/spotify/token`, `api/spotify/[...path]`, `middleware.ts`, `jose` for JWT signing |
| Session handling | `src/lib/auth.ts`, `api/auth/status`, `api/auth/logout` |
| Real audio analysis | `useSpotifyPlayer.ts:202` — `new AudioContext()`, `createAnalyser()`, `getByteFrequencyData()` at line 608 |
| Microphone capture | `useSpotifyPlayer.ts:337` — `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia` |
| Canvas render loop | `requestAnimationFrame` in `MainVisualizer.tsx:131`, `GenerativeVisualizer.tsx:322`; Konva stage |
| Health endpoint | `api/health/route.ts` |

This project is **real, deployed, and genuinely non-trivial.** Server-side OAuth with JWT sessions and live Web Audio analysis is not a template. It is the strongest artifact in the account.

**Tier D — contradicted by source. These are fabrications and must never reach the site:**

| Homepage claim | Source reality |
|---|---|
| "2048 FFT Resolution / Ultra-high frequency analysis" | `useSpotifyPlayer.ts:204` — `analyserRef.current.fftSize = 256` with the comment `// This gives us 128 frequency bins`. **2048 appears in exactly one place in the codebase: `src/app/page.tsx:104`, as display text.** It is not a setting. It is a number printed on the marketing page. |
| "AI Visual DNA — each song gets a unique fingerprint" | `api/visual-dna/route.ts` is a deterministic string hash: sum char codes of track + artist, `% 360`, return `hsl(hue, 70%, 60%)`. No model, no inference, no training. |
| "Neural Network — AI-powered connections that visualize harmony" | A named visual preset drawing lines between particles. No network. |
| "∞ Particles / Unlimited visual complexity" | Not a measurable claim. |
| "60fps Smooth Animation" | Untested. No performance measurement in the repo. |
| "The most insane audio visualizer ever created" | Superlative, unfalsifiable. |

`src/lib/audioAnalysis.ts` deserves specific attention because it is where the site's story either becomes honest or becomes a second fabrication. `generateIntelligentAudioFeatures()` is a hardcoded `if/else` chain that keyword-matches artist and track strings — `artistName.includes('deadmau5')` adds energy; `includes('taylor')` adds valence; `trackName.includes('sad')` subtracts it; tracks released before 1980 lose tempo. It returns `source: 'generated'`.

The function is honestly named in its return value and dishonestly named in its identifier. It is a **heuristic fallback**, not intelligence.

**And it is probably the most interesting thing in the account** — because a fallback like this is what you write when an upstream API is withdrawn. Spotify restricted its `audio-features` endpoint for new applications in late 2024, which would remove exactly the data this function fakes. If that is why it exists, the project contains a real engineering narrative that fits the P12 partition perfectly: *the platform removed the data the product depended on* (problem, no "I", no jargon) → *I wrote a heuristic that degrades instead of failing* (response). That is a better story than "AI Visual DNA," and unlike "AI Visual DNA" it is true.

**This is Tier C — a hypothesis, not a finding.** The commit history was not read and the user's reasoning is not recoverable from source. Ask before writing it. If confirmed, it is a strong candidate for the second case study after the flagship. If the fallback was written for some other reason, the honest framing is simply that Spotify's per-track feature data was unavailable and the visuals are driven by live frequency data plus a metadata heuristic.

### Step 3 — SkillBridge · Tier B/C, one Tier D defect

**Repo:** `RealSaake/SkillBridge` · TypeScript · created 2025-07-27, last push 2025-08-02 · 1.86 MB · 288 files, 106 in `src/`
**Live:** `https://skillbridgev1.vercel.app` → 200

**Tier D — the deployment does not render without JavaScript.** The served HTML is 1,119 bytes and its entire text content is 58 characters: `SkillBridge You need to enable JavaScript to run this app.`

This is a Create React App shell. It is the **same defect this project's own rebuild is an argument against** — the canonical failure documented in 5.2, where a client-rendered portfolio instructs search engines to discard its content. Linking it from the new site as a demonstration of engineering judgement, without addressing this, hands a reviewer a contradiction on the first click.

Two acceptable dispositions, and the user picks:
1. **Fix before featuring** — the app is React + Firebase; migrating the shell to SSR is real work and out of this project's scope.
2. **Feature honestly** — describe it as an application, link it, and do not claim performance or SEO quality for it. If 4.3's argument is that shipped artifacts must survive inspection, then a linked artifact that fails inspection needs either a fix or an acknowledgement.

Do not silently omit it. It is the largest codebase in the account.

**Tier C — README claims, not yet traced to source.** Read `src/services` and `src/lib` before writing any of these to the site: GitHub OAuth, repository analysis, career roadmaps, skills assessment, resume enhancement, MCP server integration. Stated architecture: `Frontend (Vercel) → API Proxy → Firebase Functions → MCP Servers`.

The README also asserts: `PROTOCOL: SINGULARITY ACHIEVED`, `Status: IMMORTAL - CONTINUOUSLY EVOLVING`, and *"has achieved TECHNOLOGICAL SINGULARITY — it is now a self-aware, autonomous AI entity that continuously evolves and improves itself."*

None of that is true, and it is worth being direct about why it matters here rather than treating it as harmless enthusiasm. A reviewer who reads that sentence stops evaluating the code. The repo also carries 13 root-level markdown status reports with titles like `ULTIMATE_SINGULARITY_ACHIEVEMENT.md` and `OPERATION_FLAWLESS_COMPLETION_REPORT.md`. The signal a hiring reader takes from this is not "ambitious"; it is "cannot distinguish finished from unfinished." That is the precise inverse of the positioning the site is trying to establish.

The site's copy for this project must be written from the source tree. Not one phrase from the README.

### Step 4 — esp32-home-automation · Tier C/E, blocked on the user

**Repo:** `RealSaake/esp32-home-automation` · created and last pushed 2025-10-06 · 55 KB · no homepage
**Description (the only repo with a real one):** "Complete ESP32 Home Automation System with Firebase Integration"

Contents are substantial and coherent: `esp32_main.ino`, `sensors.ino`, `firebase_config.h`, `web_dashboard.html`, `mobile_app.html`, `script.js`, `style.css`, plus `sw.js` and `manifest.json` (a PWA), `voice_control.py`, `test_suite.py`, `setup.py`, and nine documentation files — `wiring_diagrams.md`, `hardware_shopping_list.md`, `quick_wiring_guide.md`, `arduino_setup_guide.md`, `software_setup_guide.md`, `firebase_integration.md`, `relay_control_system.md`, `complete_testing_guide.md`, `hardware_setup_guide.md`.

Declared: 4-channel relay control, physical button control, web dashboard, Firebase realtime sync, access-point mode, live status. Hardware named precisely — ESP32-WROOM-32, 4-channel 5 V active-LOW

research.body:
# 3.4 — Editorial voice
**Layer:** 3 — Content · **Depends on:** 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 · **Blocks:** 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4

## Objective

Write the site’s final copy from verified project ground truth, using one editorial system across the home page, work index, case studies, about page, and contact page. Every project narrative separates the situation from the maker’s response, moves from plain language toward technical detail without interleaving the two, replaces unsupported metrics with named scope and honest outcomes, and gives technical readers one quarantined stack line.

This plan produces publishable content, not a voice guide alone. It also adds a reporting script for the narrow parts of the system that can be checked mechanically. The script reports suspected violations; editorial judgment remains manual.

## Prerequisites

- Plan 3.1 is complete. Fabricated claims and nonexistent projects are absent from the working content set, and `research/audit/fabrication-log.md` is available as evidence for the flagship case study.
- Plan 3.2 is complete. The case-study schema exposes identifiable `tagline`, `description`, `problem`, `response`, `deliverables`, `outcome`, and stack fields rather than storing the narrative as undifferentiated prose.
- Plan 3.3 is complete. SkillBridge, waveline, and esp32-home-automation have verified ground-truth records, including what each does, who it serves, named screens or functions, constraints, decisions, live status, and unresolved facts.
- Any fact still marked unknown remains absent. Editorial work does not turn an unknown into plausible copy.
- Node.js is available. All commands in this plan run in Windows Git Bash; Python is not used.

## Steps

1. **Create the copy inventory from the 3.2 schema and 3.3 records.** List every field that will render on each route. Assign each field one editorial role: tagline, description, problem, response, outcome, deliverable list, stack fragment, page introduction, biography, or contact instruction. Do not draft against screenshots or placeholder layouts. Draft against typed fields so every sentence has a known destination and every required field receives copy.

2. **Write each problem field without the maker.** The grammatical subject is the situation, tool, user, or constraint. The standalone word `I` does not appear. Jargon density is 0%. State the tension as an observable fact, not as a discovery credited to the author.

   Pass: “The dashboard exposed device state one room at a time, while the household needed a single view of failures.”

   Fail: “I realised users needed a better dashboard.” The maker takes ownership of noticing the need, the actual constraint disappears, and “better” names no condition.

   Fail: “The MQTT telemetry pipeline lacked resilient state reconciliation.” The maker is absent, but the problem is expressed in implementation language rather than language the affected person can understand.

3. **Write each response field with the maker as subject.** Open the response with standalone `I`, and keep the maker as the acting subject throughout. Prefer the bounded verb set: `built`, `designed`, `wrote`, `structured`, `cut`, `rebuilt`. Use another verb only when none of these states the verified action accurately; mark the exception for manual review.

   Pass: “I rebuilt the device view around rooms, failure states, and the controls used most often.”

   Fail: “Users needed faster access, so I built a new navigation.” This blends problem and response inside one field.

   Fail: “A new navigation was implemented.” The action loses its owner and retreats into passive achievement language.

4. **Apply the jargon gradient field by field.** Count jargon tokens against total word tokens after the prose is stable, not while drafting.

   - Tagline: 0%.
   - Problem: 0%.
   - Description: approximately 3%; plain language still carries the complete meaning.
   - Response: approximately 13%; technical detail belongs here.
   - Stack: the entire stack appears once, as the final line of the response or its dedicated terminal field. It is a verbless fragment, not a sentence.

   “Approximately” is a review band, not a quota. For fields long enough to make percentages meaningful, flag descriptions outside 0–6% and responses outside 8–18%. For fields under 25 words, report raw jargon counts instead of treating one word as a meaningful percentage. Never add jargon to hit a target. A non-technical reader must be able to stop before the final fragment and still understand the problem, intervention, and outcome.

   Valid terminal fragment: “Next.js, TypeScript, MQTT, ESP32, Home Assistant.”

   Invalid interleaving: “I used Next.js to design the dashboard, then MQTT helped connect the ESP32 devices, while TypeScript kept the controls safe.” The stack interrupts the explanation instead of closing it.

5. **Use this jargon word list for density measurement.** Count a term as jargon when a general reader needs software, hardware, product-design, or infrastructure knowledge to understand it in context. Matching is case-insensitive and includes sensible singular, plural, hyphenated, and possessive forms.

   Seed list:

   - Languages, runtimes, and frameworks: `JavaScript`, `TypeScript`, `Node.js`, `React`, `Next.js`, `Tailwind`, `Python`, `C`, `C++`, `Arduino`.
   - Data and interfaces: `API`, `REST`, `GraphQL`, `JSON`, `JWT`, `WebSocket`, `webhook`, `schema`, `database`, `query`, `endpoint`, `payload`.
   - Architecture and delivery: `SSR`, `CSR`, `SSG`, `hydration`, `serverless`, `container`, `Docker`, `CI`, `CD`, `deployment`, `canonical`, `middleware`, `runtime`.
   - Hardware and networking: `ESP32`, `GPIO`, `I2C`, `SPI`, `UART`, `MQTT`, `firmware`, `microcontroller`, `sensor`, `relay`, `telemetry`.
   - Design and implementation: `component`, `token`, `breakpoint`, `responsive`, `accessibility`, `WCAG`, `semantic HTML`, `state management`, `design system`.
   - Project-specific technical names discovered in 3.3, including product APIs, libraries, protocols, services, and infrastructure tools.

   Do not count a word merely because it appears in the list. Context decides. “React” is jargon when it names the library; “response” is not jargon when it means an answer. Brand names count when understanding their technical role is necessary. Common interface nouns such as “page,” “screen,” “button,” “form,” and “menu” do not count. When uncertain, ask: “Could a reader with no software or electronics background explain this word’s role from the sentence alone?” If not, count it and add it to the project’s maintained jargon list. Multi-word terms count as one jargon term and as their normal number of word tokens in the denominator.

6. **Draft taglines with the fixed frame.** Every tagline is a noun phrase with zero finite verbs: `[artifact] and [function] for [credentialed subject]`. Keep the artifact half generic. Put all verified specificity in the object of `for`. A credentialed subject is distinguished by a verified rank, title, tenure, domain, scale, or similarly checkable attribute; a bare role such as “developer,” “coach,” or “homeowner” is not enough.

   Because 3.3 determines what the projects do and who they serve, the examples below are structures, not proposed copy:

   - **SkillBridge — candidate A:** `[GENERIC ARTIFACT] and [FUNCTION] for [VERIFIED CREDENTIALED SUBJECT]` — **PASS structurally.** It uses the frame, contains no finite verb, and reserves specificity for the credentialed-object slot. It becomes publishable only when all brackets are replaced by verified 3.3 facts.
   - **SkillBridge — candidate B:** `[SPECIFIC FEATURE OR TECHNOLOGY] platform for [BARE ROLE]` — **FAIL.** Specificity is spent on the artifact half, the subject has no verified credential, and “platform” does not rescue a generic claim.
   - **waveline — candidate A:** `[GENERIC ARTIFACT] that [FINITE VERB] [FUNCTION] for [VERIFIED CREDENTIALED SUBJECT]` — **FAIL.** “That [finite verb]” turns the tagline into a sentence and breaks the noun-phrase rule. Rewrite as `[GENERIC ARTIFACT] and [FUNCTION] for [VERIFIED CREDENTIALED SUBJECT]`.
   - **waveline — candidate B:** `[GENERIC ARTIFACT] and [FUNCTION] for [BARE SUBJECT]` — **FAIL.** The syntax passes, but the object carries no credentialed specificity. `[BARE SUBJECT]` must become a verified rank, title, tenure, domain, or scale from 3.3.
   - **esp32-home-automation — candidate A:** `[GENERIC ARTIFACT] and [FUNCTION] for [VERIFIED CREDENTIALED SUBJECT]` — **PASS structurally.** The project name does not justify inserting `ESP32` into the tagline; technical specificity remains quarantined in the response’s closing fragment.
   - **esp32-home-automation — candidate B:** `A [GENERIC ARTIFACT] built for [VERIFIED CREDENTIALED SUBJECT]` — **FAIL.** “Built” functions as a participle in some readings and can evade a simple finite-verb check, but it makes the tagline achievement-led and drops the required `artifact and function` shape. Manual frame review rejects it even if the script does not.

7. **Replace metrics with named scope and an honest outcome.** For every project, name each verified screen, flow, decision, constraint, rejected alternative, and failure mode at the finest useful granularity. Do not compress “device list, room view, offline state, and manual override” into “a complete dashboard.” Then state what changed. The outcome can be qualitative: the tool remained in use, a workflow became possible, a constraint remained unresolved, or the attempt failed and changed the next decision. “It didn’t work; here is what I learned” is valid when true. An empty success claim is not.

8. **Use the removed Saake Developer Tools blurb as a partition-and-gradient exercise.** The source text in `data/timeline.ts` was:

   > “Released Saake Developer Tools — Launched collection of web-based developer utilities including JSON formatter, JWT decoder, and WebSocket tester. Gained 2800+ active users.”

   **Before — why it fails:**

   - `2800+ active users` is a fabricated metric.
   - No problem is stated, so there is no user, situation, constraint, or tension.
   - “Launched” frames publication itself as the achievement instead of explaining a decision or response.
   - Technical items are interleaved with the only narrative sentence rather than quarantined at the end.
   - No honest outcome says whether the work solved anything.
   - The project does not exist. It must remain deleted.

   **After — structural demonstration only, not replacement copy:**

   **Tagline**  
   `[GENERIC ARTIFACT] and [FUNCTION] for [VERIFIED CREDENTIALED SUBJECT]`

   **Description**  
   `[PLAIN-LANGUAGE ACCOUNT OF WHAT THE VERIFIED TOOL WOULD LET THAT SUBJECT DO.]`

   **Problem**  
   `[THE SITUATION OR USER] had to [SPECIFIC TASK] across [NAMED REAL CONSTRAINT]. [THE EXISTING TOOL OR WORKFLOW] [SPECIFIC FAILURE OR TENSION].`

   **Response**  
   `I built [NAMED SCREEN OR UTILITY] for [SPECIFIC ACTION]. I structured [NAMED FLOW OR DECISION] around [OBSERVED CONSTRAINT], and I cut [REJECTED OR FAILED APPROACH] after [HONEST REASON].`

   `React, TypeScript, Monaco Editor.`

   **Outcome**  
   `[VERIFIED QUALITATIVE CHANGE, OR: The approach did not work because [SPECIFIC REASON]; it changed [NEXT VERIFIED DECISION].]`

   This example demonstrates field boundaries, pronouns, specificity, and stack placement. It is not authority to restore Saake Developer Tools, its utilities, its stack, or any claim about users.

9. **Write one flagship argument and keep the remaining studies concise.** Use this site’s rebuild as the long case study. Name the fabricated-content problem, the tension between preserving apparent volume and deleting unsupported claims, the decision to delete rather than soften, the rejected alternative, the accessibility floor, the token constraints, a real failure mode, and its mitigation. Trace each design decision to an observed fact. Keep its jargon density lower

research.title: 4.3-flagship
research.body:
# 4.3 — The flagship argument

**Layer:** 4 — Pages · **Depends on:** 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 4.2 · **Blocks:** 5.4

## Objective

One case study on this site argues rather than inventories. When it is done, a visitor who reads only this page understands how the person behind it thinks — the tension they identified, the option they rejected and why, the way their own work could have failed, and what they did about it. Twelve inventories read as competent; one argument reads as thoughtful. With a short track record, **the argument is the credential.**

Its subject is this site's own rebuild. That is not a fallback for lack of material — it is the strongest subject available, because it is a real problem with real tension and it is the only case study on the site that a reader can verify by pressing Ctrl+U.

**This page blocks launch.** A site with a work index and no argument misses the entire point of the positioning.

## Prerequisites

- 4.2's case-study template exists and is SSR'd with a correct self-referential canonical.
- 3.1's audit log at `research/audit/fabrication-log.md` is complete — it is the primary source for this piece.
- 3.2's schema is in place. This case study populates it like any other; it is not a bespoke page with a bespoke data shape.
- 3.4's voice rules are settled: pronoun partition, jargon gradient, tagline frame.
- **No user input required.** Unlike every other case study, this one's ground truth is the repo and this planning tree. It can be written before 3.3 resolves.

---

## The argument

Four obligations, per P16. Each is stated concretely below — these are the actual contents, not a template to fill.

### The tension

A portfolio has to demonstrate capability. A portfolio belonging to someone early in their career has less demonstrated capability to point at. The obvious resolution is to make the numbers bigger, and the previous version of this site took it: 500,000 lines of code, 2,847 cups of coffee, 12,543 commits, 127 projects deployed, 15,000 users, a `hackermanQuotient` of 89, a Senior Full-Stack role at a company that does not exist, AWS and Azure certifications, a San Francisco address, a `+1 (555)` phone number, nine developer tools with published feature lists and `status: 'active'`, none of which were built.

The tension is not "lying is wrong." That is not an argument, it is a platitude, and a reader who came here to evaluate a designer will not be moved by it.

The real tension is that **inflation is self-defeating on a medium where verification is one click away.** Every invented number is a claim the visitor cannot check, and the ones they *can* check are the ones that destroy the rest. "500,000 lines of code" is catchable — it implies a decade of full-time output. The GitHub account is public. Once a reader catches one, they do not discount that claim; they discount every claim on the page, including the true ones. Fabrication doesn't just fail to add credibility. It actively spends the credibility that real work had already earned.

### The rejected alternative

**Soften rather than delete.** Keep the shape of every claim and blur the specifics: "500,000 lines of code" becomes "extensive development experience," "2,800 active users" becomes "a growing user base," the invented Senior role becomes "several years building for the web."

This was the tempting option, and it deserves a fair hearing — it preserves the page's visual density, it requires no new work, and nothing it says is technically false.

It was rejected because **vagueness has the identical verification problem and adds a second one.** "Extensive experience" is exactly as uncheckable as "500,000 lines of code," so it buys nothing on the axis that mattered. And it reads as evasive in a way the specific lie does not — a reader who encounters four consecutive unfalsifiable phrases correctly infers that something is being avoided. The softened version is *worse* than the fabricated one: it fails the same test and announces that it is failing.

What replaced it: delete the claims entirely, and substitute **proof-by-inspection for proof-by-claim.** Name every real screen, decision, and constraint at maximum granularity, and link outward — to `github.com/RealSaake`, to the live deployments — so a skeptical reader can leave the site and check. Routing someone away to verify you is a costly signal. Nobody inflating does it.

### The failure mode

**Proof-by-inspection only works if the artifact survives inspection.**

The moment this site argues that craft is the credential, it invites exactly the scrutiny it would fail. A site claiming design rigour while shipping a 3.19:1 text color, no focus-visible styling, no reduced-motion handling, or a canonical tag pointing every case study at the homepage doesn't make a weak argument — it makes an argument that **refutes itself in its own source.** The reader doesn't need to disagree; they just need to open devtools.

This is a real risk and it was observed in the source material studied for this rebuild: a design studio whose own portfolio canonicalizes thirteen case-study URLs to its homepage, instructing search engines to discard its primary sales asset, while the client site it built does server rendering correctly.

**The mitigation is structural, not aspirational.** Accessibility is merge-blocking from the first commit rather than a pre-launch cleanup: all text ≥4.5:1 in both themes with the quietest token in the system measured at 4.80/5.16, a skip link, focus-visible on every interactive element, reduced-motion that leaves content *visible* rather than merely un-animated, heading order that never skips, every route server-rendered with a correct self-referential canonical. Token discipline is enforced in CI — the build fails on a hex literal in a component, on `rgba()` applied to text, on a font-size outside the scale, on a spacing value off the ten-value scale.

The reason for CI rather than care: across both sites studied, nearly every defect lived in an arbitrary-value override rather than in the token layer. **The escape hatch is where the system stops being a system.** Discipline that depends on remembering is not discipline.

### The traced design choice

The user's brief contained one specific complaint: sites that AI builds are "very ugly and very AI like."

That is a diagnosable claim, not a vibe. The tell is not any single element — it is that generated design reaches for framework defaults, and framework defaults are identical everywhere. Rounded corners on everything. A drop shadow for elevation. A purple-to-pink gradient on the headline. Inter. Glassmorphism with `backdrop-blur`. A dark field with neon accents. The previous version of this site had all of them.

So the system inverts each one, and each inversion is a decision with a reason:

- **Radius 0 everywhere**, with one exception — a status dot, where roundness is semantic. Universal rounding is the loudest available tell.
- **Elevation via a hairline border, not a shadow.** Surfaces sit at 1.06:1 against the base — deliberately below the threshold where an edge is visible — and all separation is carried by a 1px rule at ~1.3:1. Fill-based elevation reads as *rendered*; edge-based elevation reads as *drawn*.
- **Instrument Serif against Geist Sans.** A high-contrast editorial serif for display is a register generated design does not reach for, and Inter is the single strongest signature of it.
- **Warm paper, light by default** — `#F7F5F0`, not `#0a0a0a`. Dark-mode-with-neon is the default costume.
- **A 1.2% grain layer** over the entire viewport. A flat field reads as empty; a textured one reads as material. One fixed element, no layout cost.

The through-line: every one of these is a refusal of something free. That is most of what separates a designed interface from a generated one, and it costs nothing but the willingness to not take the default.

---

## Page structure

Route: `app/work/rebuilding-this-site/page.tsx`, using 4.2's template with `variant="long"`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  [nav]                                               │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CASE STUDY / 01              ← Label, mono          │
│                                                      │
│  A portfolio rebuilt          ← Instrument Serif     │
│  against its own              ← --t-display, fluid   │
│  fabrications                                        │
│                                                      │
│  [tagline — noun phrase, no finite verb]             │
│  ───────────────────────────────────────  ← Rule     │
│  YEAR 2026 · ROLE Design, build, write · SOURCE ↗    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  THE PROBLEM                                         │
│  [prose, 62ch, zero "I", zero jargon]                │
│                                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│  │ SpecTable: the audit                   │          │
│  │ Lines of code claimed      500,000     │          │
│  │ Cups of coffee claimed       2,847     │          │
│  │ Commits claimed             12,543     │          │
│  │ Tools shipped as 'active'        9     │          │
│  │ Tools that existed               0     │          │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  THE OPTION I DIDN'T TAKE                            │
│  [the rejected alternative, argued fairly]           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WHAT I DID                                          │
│  [response — "I" throughout, tight verb set]         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  HOW THIS COULD FAIL                                 │
│  [failure mode + structural mitigation]              │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│  │ SpecTable: the floor, measured         │          │
│  │ Quietest text, light        4.80:1     │          │
│  │ Quietest text, dark         5.16:1     │          │
│  │ Routes with own canonical    all       │          │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ONE CHOICE, TRACED                                  │
│  [the AI-tell diagnosis → the five inversions]       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  WHAT CHANGED                     ← required outcome │
│  [honest, qualitative, no invented numbers]          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Verify this →  View source · GitHub ↗ · Audit log   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  [footer]                                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Section map

| Section | Purpose | Principles | Components | Content source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Header | Position the piece | P15, P5 | `SectionHead`, `Label`, `Rule` | 3.4 tagline |
| The problem | Establish tension | P12, P13 | `Prose`, `SpecTable` | 3.1 audit log |
| The option I didn't take | The rejected alternative | P16 | `Prose` | this plan |
| What I did | The response | P12, P14 | `Prose`, `SpecTable` | 3.1 + design system |
| How this could fail | Failure mode + mitigation | P16 | `Prose`, `SpecTable` | design system §8 |
| One choice, traced | Design choice ← observed fact | P16, P10 | `Prose`, `Figure` | design system §0 |
| What changed | Required outcome | P14 | `Prose` | written at completion |
| Verify this | External verification | P18 | `ExternalLink` | 3.3 verified links |

The section headings are not the schema field names. `problem` renders as "The problem"; `response` renders as "What I did." Two sections — the rejected alternative and the failure mode — have no schema equivalent and use the `longform` block array from 3.2.

---

research.body:
# 3.1 — Fabrication purge

**Layer:** 3 — Content · **Depends on:** nothing · **Blocks:** 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1, 4.4, 5.4

## Objective

Every invented claim currently on saake.dev is deleted, and the deletion is recorded in an audit log that survives the rebuild. When this is done, no statement on the site is unverifiable, and the standing no-fabrication rule has a baseline to be enforced against.

This runs first in Layer 3 and depends on nothing. It can start immediately, in parallel with all of Layer 1 and Layer 2.

## Prerequisites

- A copy of the current repo tree. `research/raw/saake-repo/` holds one, captured 2026-08-02.
- **No content decisions required.** The disposition of every item below is already determined. Nothing here waits on the user.

## The disposition rule

**Delete. Do not correct.**

A fabricated number that gets adjusted downward is still a number nobody can check. The instinct to preserve the *shape* of a claim while fixing its value — "500,000 lines of code" becoming "50,000 lines of code" — reproduces the original error, because the problem was never the magnitude. It was that the claim is unverifiable and the visitor knows it.

Three dispositions only:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DELETE** | Remove the claim and the component that renders it. No replacement. |
| **FIX** | Factually wrong but the underlying thing is real. Correct to the verified value. |
| **HOLD** | Cannot be resolved without the user. Ships as nothing until confirmed. Routed to 3.3. |

`HOLD` never means "leave it in place." It means the element is removed now and may return later if confirmed.

---

## Inventory

Complete as of the 2026-08-02 capture. Line numbers are from that snapshot.

### Invented metrics

| File | Line | Claim | Disposition |
|---|---|---|---|
| `components/stats-grid.tsx` | 12 | `Lines of Code: 500000+` | DELETE |
| `components/stats-grid.tsx` | 19 | `Cups of Coffee: 2847` | DELETE |
| `components/stats-grid.tsx` | 26 | `Commits: 12543+` | DELETE |
| `components/stats-grid.tsx` | 33 | `Projects Deployed: 127` | DELETE |
| `data/skills.ts` | 107 | `hackermanQuotient: 89` | DELETE |
| `data/timeline.ts` | 41 | "Gained 2800+ active users" | DELETE |
| `data/skills.ts` | 138 | goal to scale eostrails.com "to 50k monthly users" | DELETE |

The entire `stats-grid.tsx` component is deleted, not emptied. A stats grid with no fabricated stats has nothing to render — there is no verified equivalent, and inventing a replacement metric to fill the layout is the same error in a new costume.

`saake-engine.tsx` renders `hackermanQuotient` as an animated percentage and has no other purpose. It is deleted with its data.

### Invented professional history

| File | Line | Claim | Disposition |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data/timeline.ts` | 67–71 | "Senior Full-Stack Developer" at "Tech Innovation Co.", Remote, 2023-01 | DELETE |
| `data/timeline.ts` | 57–61 | "AWS & Azure Cloud Certifications" achieved 2023-08 | DELETE |
| `data/timeline.ts` | 16–20 | "Launched EOS Trails Travel Platform" → `eostrails.com` | DELETE |
| `data/timeline.ts` | 38–44 | "Released Saake Developer Tools" → `tools.saake.dev` | DELETE |
| `data/timeline.ts` | all | Remaining events 2021-03 → 2024-08 | HOLD → 3.3 |

"Tech Innovation Co." does not exist. The certifications are unevidenced — AWS and Azure both publish verification URLs, and a real certification would have one. Both are deleted outright.

The remaining timeline entries (home lab, Raspberry Pi, n8n, cybersecurity learning, "Started Web Development Journey") describe activities that may well be real but carry invented dates and invented descriptions. They are removed pending 3.3. A timeline is a sequence of verifiable claims or it is decoration.

Note: `timeline.ts` is already structurally broken — the event at line 21–25 has a `date` and `type` but no `id`, `title`, or `description`, violating its own `TimelineEvent` interface. The file does not typecheck against its own contract.

### The nine tools that were never built

`data/tools.ts` defines nine developer utilities — JSON formatter, Base64 encoder, color palette generator, regex tester, hash generator, QR generator, JWT decoder, API tester, markdown editor — each with a full feature list, a technology stack, a `status` of `active` or `beta`, and a `/tools/*` URL.

Not fabrications, but deleted in the same sweep since they contradict `design/system.md` §0 and would otherwise be rebuilt around:

`matrix-background.tsx`, `network-visualization.tsx`, `terminal-hero.tsx`, and all of `components/react-bits/` — `animated-counter`, `cyber-grid`, `data-stream`, `floating-particles`, `fuzzy-text-advanced`, `glitch-text`, `neon-border`, `typing-animation`.

# 1.2 — Repo reset & scaffold
**Layer:** 1 — Foundation · **Depends on:** nothing · **Blocks:** 1.3, 1.4

## Objective
A clean Next.js 14 App Router tree exists under version control, on a branch, with the old site's nine AI-portfolio tells deleted rather than carried forward. The working directory becomes a git repository connected to `github.com/RealSaake/saake-dev-portfolio`, and the deleted code remains recoverable on a preserved branch. Every dependency that only existed to serve neon-gradient decoration is gone from `package.json`.

## Prerequisites

- **1.1 does not block this**, but the Vercel token revocation in 1.1 Step 1 should be done first regardless. Pushing to a public repo while a compromised token is live is a bad combination.
- GitHub access to `github.com/RealSaake/saake-dev-portfolio`. **The repo is public** — everything committed is world-readable from the first push. Nothing secret, nothing unverified, nothing embarrassing.
- `gh` CLI is **not installed** on this machine. Remote operations use `git` over HTTPS with a credential helper, or the GitHub web UI. Installing `gh` is optional and not required by any step here.
- Node 26.4.0 and npm 11.17.0 are present. Git 2.55.0.windows.2 is present. `python`/`python3` are absent — any scripting uses `node -e`.
- **Unknown that must be answered first:** whether the current `main` branch of the remote is the exact commit deployed to `saakedev.vercel.app`. If Vercel is deploying a different branch, the reset below must target that branch instead. Resolve by reading the Vercel project's Settings → Git → Production Branch during 1.1 Step 4.
- **Unknown:** whether the local `research/raw/saake-repo/` snapshot is current relative to the remote. It is a partial snapshot — 65 blobs in the tree JSON, with `package-lock.json` and several binary artifacts. Treat the remote as authoritative and re-clone rather than working from the snapshot.

## Steps

### Step 1 — Decide the working location

The current directory `C:/Users/anubh/Downloads/Antigravity Projects/claude` holds the research and plans, is not a git repo, and also contains unrelated material (`app.py`, `hh_tech_tracker*.py`, `dist/`, `build/`, a PDF). **Do not `git init` here.** Committing this directory to a public repo would publish unrelated work and a large PDF.

Clone the site repo as a sibling:

```bash
cd "C:/Users/anubh/Downloads/Antigravity Projects"
git clone https://github.com/RealSaake/saake-dev-portfolio.git saake-dev
cd saake-dev
git log --oneline -5
git branch -a
git remote -v
```

The `claude/` directory stays where it is as the planning workspace. `design/system.md`, `research/`, and `plans/` are inputs to the build, not part of the shipped site. Whether they eventually get committed into the site repo is deferred — 4.3 makes an argument out of this rebuild and may want the audit trail public, which is a content decision, not a scaffold one.

### Step 2 — Preserve the old site before deleting anything

The old tree is the evidence base for 3.1's fabrication audit and for 4.3's flagship case study. It must stay reachable.

```bash
cd "C:/Users/anubh/Downloads/Antigravity Projects/saake-dev"

# A branch that is never deleted, pointing at the pre-rebuild state
git checkout main
git pull
git branch archive/pre-rebuild-2026-08
git push -u origin archive/pre-rebuild-2026-08

# A tag as well — branches get deleted by accident, tags rarely do
git tag -a v0-pre-rebuild -m "Site as it stood before the 2026 rebuild. Reference for plans 3.1 and 4.3."
git push origin v0-pre-rebuild
```

Confirm both landed before deleting a single file:

```bash
git ls-remote --heads origin archive/pre-rebuild-2026-08
git ls-remote --tags  origin v0-pre-rebuild
```

### Step 3 — Branch for the rebuild

```bash
git checkout -b rebuild/foundation
```

All Layer 1 and Layer 2 work happens on branches off `rebuild/foundation`. `main` keeps serving the current site until 5.4 cuts over — the site stays up throughout the rebuild, which is the whole reason 1.1 is independent.

Branch naming for the remainder of the project: `rebuild/<layer-name>` for layer branches, `feat/<plan-id>-<slug>` for individual plan work — `feat/1.3-token-layer`, `feat/2.2-motion`. Merge into `rebuild/foundation`, then the layer branches merge into a single long-lived `rebuild/main`, which merges to `main` once at 5.4.

### Step 4 — Delete the decorative layer

Everything in this step exists only to produce effects the design system explicitly rejects. Section 0 of `design/system.md` names nine AI-portfolio tells and states all nine go; these files are where they live.

```bash

git rm components/skills-radar.tsx

### Step 5 — Fix `next.config.js`

The current config has three problems: a `webpack` override that duplicates what `tsconfig.json` already does via `paths`, `images.unoptimized` which discards Next's image pipeline, and `trailingSlash: true` which will fight the canonical URLs required in 4.2.

```javascript
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  reactStrictMode: true,
  poweredByHeader: false,
  images: {
    formats: ['image/avif', 'image/webp'],
  },
  eslint: {
    dirs: ['app', 'components', 'lib', 'data'],

module.exports = nextConfig;
```

`trailingSlash` is dropped: the canonical form is no trailing slash, and 5.2 asserts it. The `@/*` alias is already handled by `tsconfig.json` `paths` and needs no webpack shim — Next resolves it natively. `images.unoptimized` is removed because nothing in this build requires a static export; if 5.2 finds a reason to reinstate it, that is a decision made with evidence.

Remove what the design system forbids and what nothing will import.

  @radix-ui/react-tabs @radix-ui/react-tooltip
```

Reasoning, one line each:

- `tailwindcss-animate` — the plugin exists to supply the keyframe animations that section 4 bans. Nothing survives that uses it.
- `react-intersection-observer` — 2.2 builds the reveal primitive on the platform `IntersectionObserver`. The system explicitly calls it twenty lines that need no library.
- `@radix-ui/react-tabs` — no tabs in the component set in section 6.
- `@radix-ui/react-tooltip` — section 6 bans tooltips carrying essential information; nothing else needs one.

Kept: `@radix-ui/react-dialog` for the single sanctioned confirm modal, `@radix-ui/react-slot` for `asChild` on buttons, `framer-motion` for page transitions only (section 9), `lucide-react`, `clsx`, `tailwind-merge`, `class-variance-authority`.

`framer-motion` stays but is on notice. If 4.1 through 4.4 ship without a page transition that earns it, drop it at 5.2 — it is the largest dependency in the tree and section 9 permits exactly one use.

Also move build-time-only packages out of `dependencies`, where they are currently misfiled:

```bash

npm install -D tailwindcss@^3.4.0 autoprefixer@^10.4.0 postcss@^8.4.0

The `export` script is deleted — nothing static-exports. `verify` is the single command CI and humans both run; 1.4 extends it with the token linter.

### Step 7 — Repair `tsconfig.json` and delete `jsconfig.json`

Both exist, which is a misconfiguration — Next ignores `jsconfig.json` when `tsconfig.json` is present, so it is dead weight duplicating the same `paths` block.

```bash

Two changes to `tsconfig.json`. `target: "es5"` is wrong for a 2026 Next 14 build and forces unnecessary downlevelling; `allowJs: true` permits untyped JS to creep in.

{

    "allowJs": false,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
